utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. My name is Djuro Cepic, and I am counsel for Lazarevic. And I will be addressing ground one of our appeal brief. Can we have slide one in front of us on the screen, and I would like the usher's assistance to distribute a copy of the document to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you very much, Your Honour. [Interpretation] When addressing the crime base, I would like to point out that in item 1 of our appeals brief we have explained in detail that members of the Army of Yugoslavia did conduct themselves in keeping with the law and constitution and those who broke the law were prosecuted by the competent bodies. An important issue arises, which is the alleged conveyance of oral orders to commit crimes. My learned friend Mr. Kremer raised this very issue the day before yesterday and this can be found at Volume III, paragraph 43, of the trial judgement. In their appeals brief, the Defence indicated what the contradictory elements were in the testimony of this witness and directed the attention to the fact that it absolutely lacks credibility and is inadmissible. And at this stage we would only like to show the most glaring example of it to Their Honours. We have a slide in front of us which is the contents of the K90 testimony, where he clearly says that he had never been ordered to commit any crimes against villagers. Can we have slide two, please. As you can see, this is corroborated by other testimonies and Judge Bonomy, the Presiding Judge himself, made a very clear conclusion about this witness which we can see at the bottom of this slide; and the reference is transcript page 9489. Hence, these portions of the transcript clearly show that Witness K90 was not a credible or reliable witness and that he changed his written statement significantly in the course of his testimony. Therefore, the Trial Chamber had to reject the testimony of this witness. On the other hand, had it assessed his testimony at all, it would have had to reach a completely different finding from the one it did in the trial judgement; that is to say that there was no such general pattern. Another illogical point of his testimony is that he himself was a soldier and that he could not possibly know in which way the orders were conveyed down the chain. That the orders were conveyed down the chain of command in keeping with the law is clearly shown by the fact that the Prosecution investigator, Philip Coo, upon his arrival in Belgrade, found the entire documentation of the Army of Yugoslavia from the relevant period in the archives. The reference is 12075 of the transcript. And on the basis of all these documents and combat reports he, and later on the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber after the evidence was adduced, could make a complete and thorough analysis of the relevant events rather than have the Trial Chamber's findings be based on indirect evidence on the principle of pick and choose; whereas, on the other hand, there was ample evidence adduced which lead to reasonable findings in the favour of the Defence which was not taken into consideration in adjudication. Furthermore, I'd like to point the fact -- point out the fact that there were over 30 chains of command under the Pristina Corps. This fact clearly shows that in the event that there had been the procedure of verbally handing down orders, this would have completely disrupted these chains of command. Can I have the next slide, please. I would now like to address the crime base and some findings of the Trial Chamber on this score. The Trial Chamber erred in finding that none of the reports of the subordinate units which speak about the large numbers of displaced Kosovo Albanians and the engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in connection with their movement and provisions for them do not relate to the locations where, according to the Trial Chamber finding, the forcible displacement by the VJ was found. This is Volume III, paragraph 912. Such a finding has no basis and is contradictory to the findings of the Trial Chamber itself in that same judgement and in -- and is also contrary to ample adduced evidence. As you can see on this slide, you have on the left-hand side the finding of the Trial Chamber and on the right-hand side the finding reached by the Trial Chamber in Volume III, paragraph 905, which deals with the humane treatment by VJ members in the areas between the villages of Turicevac, Izbica, Vocnjak, and Cirez in late March 1999. [In English] At the end of March of 1999. Yes, thank you. [Interpretation] It is a showing of how the VJ forces stopped their actions precisely for the sake of protecting civilians and the instance where a senior officer from the Pristina Corps itself had arrived to assist this activity. This was corroborated by testimonies and the combat report of the units of the VJ which is P2046. Can I have the next slide, please. We will continue addressing the municipality of Srbica. In addition to the Trial Chamber finding, I would like to point to other evidence relating to this area and the relevant time which are clearly in favour of the Defence. We have explained in our appeal brief that the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia did not enter the village of Cirez in the period of time when allegedly crimes were found to have been committed there. But, as you can see in the slide, after the subsequent arrival of the army in the area we can clearly see that -- what sort of attitude the members of the VJ had toward the civilians. These are all testimonies of Prosecution witnesses, assistance in food, medication, and other forms of assistance that could have been provided by soldiers. Can I have the next slide, please. The orders and reports of the Yugoslav Army in the area of Srbica clearly show that the soldiers under the command of General Lazarevic treated civilians humanely. As you can see, there is even a relevant portion of this -- the Trial Chamber -- the exhibits -- 5D1033, this is the 37th Brigade report about the protection of civilians in the area; next Exhibit 5D1083, the report of the 37th Brigade of the army, which sought measures to be undertaken for the protection of civilians, the securing of a supply of food and other necessities; 5D1037, a report about the situation in Glogovac, where the Red Cross is called upon to provide assistance; 5D105D [as interpreted], where the army distributed its own food reserves to help the civilians. That's to say all the civilians present in the area regardless of their faith or ethnicity, and I'd like to say that under all the censuses Glogovac was 99 per cent Albanian. [In English] Sorry for intervention. Page 7, line 1, it could be -- it has to be 5D1059, exhibit number. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Can I have the next slide. We have two maps before us. One was admitted as evidence. A credible Prosecution witness, Colonel Bislim Zyrapi, the chief of the KLA staff in the relevant period. And on the other side we have a map IC157; it is a Defence witness's map, Colonel Dikovic's map, who was present in the area in the relevant period. Colonel Zyrapi's map is IC105. These maps are consistent in the essential parts and the testimony by Witness Bislim Zyrapi clearly shows that there was fighting between the VJ and law enforcement forces on the one hand and the KLA on the other. In his credible testimony Colonel Zyrapi explained that the area was under the control of his forces. In addition to that, he said the following, and I will quote, this is transcript page 6003, lines 5 to 6: [In English] "It was normal for us to order the movement of the population but also of the KLA ..." [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber found in the example of Belanica that there was not a war crime committed, precisely thanks to such a position held by Colonel Zyrapi and if we know that Colonel Zyrapi testified that this was a principle which applied to the entire territory of Kosovo, then this direct piece of evidence will lead us to the conclusion of what the general pattern was. I would particularly like to thank the Appeals Chamber for its order of the 20th of February, in which it pointed out the question of the location of the alleged crime, the village of Tusilje, the 29th of March, 1999. As a matter of fact, in the indictment that village was not pointed out, and therefore there is -- there are no grounds for its presence in the judgement because that would mean going beyond the scope of the indictment. Now I'd like to ask my colleague Mr. Cvijic to play a video-clip that was played during the trial as well. It is a night of bombing in Pristina, one of the many nights of bombing, that is the 7th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see it. Buildings aflame. You see residential buildings that were hit. The question is whether any of the people living in this building would stay on after this kind of bombing. And I would like to note that during the bombing 199 projectiles hit the town of Pristina only, hitting civilian targets at that. Now that we're speaking of Pristina, I wish to repeat what my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman pointed out yesterday. In Pristina there were no combat units of the VJ. All the combat units were defending the country outside of town. This was attested to by the war commanders, also the Defence Witness Filipovic and also there are many combat reports to that effect of the Army of Yugoslavia. As I've already pointed out earlier, the archives were complete. Each and every combat report could have been found. And any movement by units could have been reconstructed. What I wish to point out to the Appeals Chamber is that in Pristina in the outskirts humanitarian aid was provided to civilians by the VJ and that is attested to by many documents. PD499 [as interpreted], as you can see, the 354th Brigade of the army is taking care of 15.000 ethnic Albanians who were returning, and they were put up in Ladovac and Sajkovac. 5D615, the 211th Brigade is providing humanitarian aid to the Albanian population and everything else they may have needed. Even Colonel Zlatomir Pesic, a Prosecution witness, commander of the military district in Pristina, pointed out that he tried to keep a group of civilians at their homes. Also we have 5D592 where we see that members of the 211th Brigade of the VJ provided medical assistance to the civilian population. Could I please have the next slide now. I shall briefly deal with the municipality of Prizren as well. We see here that there are several orders and several combat reports. We see what the attitude was. My colleague Mr. Ackerman pointed out yesterday that some refugee columns were hit by NATO bombs. As you can see in report 5D1158, NATO projectiles hit a refugee column in the territory of the municipality of Prizren and further on the municipality of Djakovica. There was a vast number of victims. People were killed, wounded, and here we see that the members of the Army of Yugoslavia offered assistance to civilian victims of NATO bombing. And Defence Witness Franjo Gloncak pointed that out. Then also this happened near the village of Korisa. The first example I provided is in the village of Pirane and in the crime base it says that it was in Pirane that there was forcible deportation of the civilians. The statement by Witness Gloncak is 5D1395. In addition to that, the same witness describes the situation when a civilian column was hit by 15 NATO projectiles. This was a column of Albanian refugees that were returning to their homes near the village of Korisa, the municipality of Prizren. As you can see, hundreds of victims. Witness Gloncak gave his own blood to help the civilians who were harmed. All of this is corroborated by 5D194 [as interpreted] of the 549th Brigade about that attack. Could we please have the next slide now. This is testimony provided by Prosecution witnesses, K79. The army returned civilians to their homes wherever they could. 9721 is the transcript page. General Maisonneuve also praised the conduct of the VJ in the area and also there is ample evidence that we provided in our brief that testifies to this humane treatment. Could we please have the next slide now. The situation was the same in the municipality of Djakovica, 5D1158, the wounded in the column that we mentioned in the municipality of Djakovica, medical team -- a military medical team is being sent to help them, although that is not the task of the army. Of course the army is defending the country respecting the law, but it is other structures that are taking care of civilians. 5D1147 also speaks about taking care of civilians. Could I please have the next slide now. Document PD1147 and PD1144 and PD1155 [as interpreted]. Now we are moving on to the municipality of Orahovac. There is also a reference here to the humane treatment provided by the Army of Yugoslavia. There is a reference to Witness K79 who also says that the army acted in accordance with the law. Could we please have the next page -- the next slide, rather. And we see numerous documents like 5D963, speaking of humanitarian aid provided to civilians. 5D964, 5D1071, where it says that civilians in that area were fully protected. There are also many other documents there, like 5D1072, 973, 974, and so on. Thank you. As I've already explained using the example of Srbica, the situation was the same in the municipalities of Djakovica, Prizren, and Orahovac. On the left-hand side we have Colonel Delic's map, IC1515, and on the right-hand side we have Colonel Zyrapi's map. He was the Chief of Staff of the KLA, P2447. The movements of units coincide to a large extent and Colonel Zyrapi explains the fighting that took place there as he explained in the case of Srbica as well. As we said in our brief, near the village of Pirane, near the village of Celine there was fighting between the KLA forces on the one hand and the forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia on the other. Transcript reference 5991 and 5992. Next, please, that is map P2447. This is Colonel Zyrapi's map and he shows here the area that was under their control on the 25th of March and the alleged crime base is marked in these locations, but as I've already said Colonel Zyrapi explained that they ordered movement by the civilian population and he also said that there was fighting between the two warring parties. Also, I wish to add to that that this was under constant NATO bombing and hundreds and hundreds of projectiles fell in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. All of this clearly indicates that the specific direction of all these actions taken by the army pertain to the defence of the country in an exceptionally difficult situation due to the NATO bombing and simultaneous heavy fighting with the KLA. Your Honours, with your leave, now I would like to deal with the first question from your order dated the 20th of February, this year, and it has to do with disciplinary and other measures that were taken in relation to the members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Could we please have the next slide now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, can I give you a piece of advice?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that you have to point out for us where the Trial Chamber is wrong in the judgement as error of law and error of facts instead of repeating the evidence you showed during the trial stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We pointed all these paragraphs from the judgement and all relevant exhibits in our appeal brief, and I was thinking that this presentation should be just to present that argument in some additional light. So that is the point of that presentation. We do have everything filed in our appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. But bear my remarks in mind in your further submissions. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In this way I wish to respond to your question specifically from your order of the 20th of February, and it has to do with the following: Whether the Trial Chamber erred when they found that General Lazarevic had not taken sufficient measures that particularly pertained to his contribution to the crime of deportation and other -- his failure to take adequate measures to ensure the proper investigation of serious crimes committed by the VJ. This is Volume III, paragraph 900. I hope that I'm assisting the Appeals Chamber in this way. As a matter of fact, such a ruling by the Chamber simply does not hold water, to put it mildly. General Lazarevic did his very best at the time that is relevant to the indictment. When we're speaking of disciplinary responsibility we have some provisions of the Law on The Army of Yugoslavia - that is P984 and Article 159 - clearly defines what disciplinary measures are as much. In this way I wish to refer to the appeals judgement in Gotovina and Markac, paragraph 133. The Chamber concluded that the accused had taken disciplinary measures against a large number of soldiers and that was in their favour. What I am going to show to you now is that General Lazarevic did that exactly and even more than that within the scope of his possibilities, but first we have to deal with the key issue. For all of us who deal in criminal law, this is the primary issue; that is, disciplinary responsibility as responsibility for set work obligations and, therefore, that is a much lower form of responsibility than criminal liability. In disciplinary proceedings someone cannot be held accountable for crimes of murder, rape, deportation, or any other crime or war crime. Aleksandar Vasiljevic, Prosecution witness, explained that in a specific example; 8968 is the transcript reference. Next slide, please. As you can see, there are clear-cut disciplinary sanctions that are spelled out in Articles 163 and 164 and the most serious sanction is 20 days in military detention. We will agree that we are not going to punish in that way someone who committed a crime. In addition to that there is Article 181 of the Army of Yugoslavia that says that the military disciplinary court, disciplinary proceedings before military courts, have to be taken by army commanders, that is the lowest level. Also, Article 204, paragraph 2 of the Army of Yugoslavia, says that in a case of war, in a war situation, as a rule disciplinary measures or disciplinary sentences the implementation of which is not feasible or possible shall not be handed down during the state of war. However, in spite of such limitations, General Lazarevic took all measures that were within the scope of his possibilities with a view to punishing soldiers in accordance with the law - 5D260, March 1999, 12th of March, 1999 - and he is asking for strict disciplinary measures to be taken. Then we also see from PD1144 [as interpreted] that again General Lazarevic asked for that and on the 29th of March, 1999, and also there were criminal sanctions involved too. Then also document P2029 of the 1st of April, 1999, and then 4D237 of the 7th of May, 1999. There are also numerous documents of subordinate units stating that these measures were being taken. I am going to refer to some of them: 5D1293, 5D1020, 5D554, 5D365, 5D388, 5D387, 5D315, 5D550, 5D798, 5D1142, 5D1151, 5D1154. Could we look at the next slide, please. What is the most important thing is, as I said, disciplinary violations are taken from minor violations. If somebody is late for work, if they did not turn up to the unit in time, if they mildly infringe on military discipline. But what is most significant in this case is the criminal prosecution of perpetrators of criminal acts. My colleague, Mr. Bakrac, will speak more about that. All I would like to point out is that military officers, superior officers, and the corps commander himself carried out their duties by submitting criminal reports because the courts and the prosecutor's offices are independent in their work in the same way that this Court and this Prosecutor's office are independent in their work. In the same way the courts in the area of Yugoslavia and the territory of Serbia by constitution and by law were defined. Their functions were defined. In front of us we see Article 143 [as interpreted] of the constitution and we see also the article on the work of military courts which defines their independence. I would also like to say that members of the Pristina Corps in the time relevant for this judgement submitted 2.382 criminal reports, of which one-fifth referred to violations of international humanitarian law. This was in 492 criminal reports filed. I tried to find in the jurisprudence of this and other criminal courts that deal with war crimes similar examples of this volume of prosecution and the extent to which humane measures were taken in respect of civilians and I was not successful in that. I didn't manage to find any, which clearly speaks to the fact that General Lazarevic subordinated the principle of military efficiency to the principle of humaneness. And that he adhered to the constitution and the law in all his actions that he was bound by, by rules and regulations. I would like to thank you for your attention and my colleague, Mr. Bakrac, will continue with our presentation.

utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be addressing the gist of our grounds of appeal, numbers two and three. In relation to these grounds of appeal, the Defence will be specifically addressing the questions put by Their Honours, numbers two and three, from the 20 February 2013 order of this Appeals Chamber. With all due respect, our Defence submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that General Vladimir Lazarevic participated in aiding and abetting the deportations and forcible transfers of the Albanian population and that his actus reus in these actions consisted of the following: Under one, participation in the planning and the execution of joint VJ and MUP operations; under two, issuance of Grom 3 and Grom 4 orders and Joint Command orders which sent the VJ into actions in those locations where the forcible displacement of Albanians occurred; under three, his presence in the field and inspection of units which boosted the combat morale of soldiers; and lastly, under four, his failure to take adequate measures to secure the proper investigation of the serious crimes committed by the Army of Yugoslavia. These Trial Chamber's findings can be found in the trial judgement, Volume III, paragraph 925. The Defence reiterates that in our view and in view of the totality of the evidence adduced in this case the Trial Chamber completely erred in this finding. In order to reach the finding that through these actions General Lazarevic aided and abetted the deportations and forcible transfer of the Albanian population, it was incumbent upon the Trial Chamber in keeping with what we believe is now the prevailing jurisprudence of the ICTY to establish the so-called specific direction of these actions as the decisive element of actus reus for aiding and abetting. It was necessary to establish this specific direction explicitly in our view in order to establish the necessary link between the acts of aiding and the crimes committed by principal perpetrators. In order to establish the existence of specific direction in the actions by General Lazarevic, the Trial Chamber was obligated to properly establish the broad context in which these actions were done. And it was precisely at this crucial stage that the Trial Chamber erred. Because of the erroneous interpretation of the evidence adduced and possible prejudice, instead of finding that General Lazarevic as an honourable officer and professional acted in keeping with his constitutional, legal, and moral obligation to defend his country from the KLA and NATO campaign, the Trial Chamber instead found that General Lazarevic, in fact, aided and abetted deportations and forcible transfer of the Albanian population. The extent to which the erroneous understanding of this general context of events and the constitutionally and legally established laws and obligations that Lazarevic had as the Pristina Corps commander affected the erroneous reasoning of the Trial Chamber is best illustrated by the evidence which was adduced at trial and which was -- which the Trial Chamber gave a completely different meaning from the one that a reasonable trier of fact would. The acts that the appellant did to defend the country were interpreted by the Chamber as aiding and abetting a crime. And these errors of fact have, in fact, occasioned a miscarriage of justice. We will now address each and every one of these elements of actus reus of aiding and abetting and we'll find that they militate in General Lazarevic's favour. We will now first deal with the planning and execution of joint VJ and MUP actions. The Defence notes that in the context of the events in Kosovo in the relevant period, the participation in the planning and execution of joint VJ and MUP actions in Kosovo was not just lawful but also logical and necessary. The Defence could not find anywhere in the trial judgement a clear distinction between this legitimate, logical, and necessary actions on the part of the appellant and those acts or omissions which would clearly and unequivocally show that what was done was with the intent on the part of the appellant to aid and abet deportations and forcible transfers. The appellant was a corps commander in the relevant period of time and his main task was on the basis of the orders of the superior command to plan actions for the defence of the country from the KLA and the NATO campaign. It was, therefore, incumbent on the Trial Chamber to show unequivocally and make a clear distinction between what were the lawful and the regular professional tasks of the appellant and those acts in the planning and execution of joint acts which would show that they had been done in such a way as to amount to a significant contribution to the commission of these crimes and that the appellant was aware of it. In all lines of work, including those of a general in command of a corps, there exists a description of duties and one of these duties on the part of a general is to plan operations, especially so in a state of war. Is that punishable? Certainly not. I would now invite you to look at a slide where we will only summarise the views presented by Prosecution witnesses, those witnesses who in view of their experience and position were well-placed to state certain things about this. Among them were quite a few high-ranking officials of international organisations, and in respect of these elements that the Trial Chamber held amounted to the actus reus on the part of the appellant, they stated that these actions were, in fact, legal and legitimate. And what's more, that they were necessary where the country was defending itself from the KLA and the NATO campaign. So according to the Prosecution Witness Maisonneuve the co-ordination between the VJ and the MUP was more than necessary, it was highly professional. Every operation which implies the participation of both the VJ and MUP had to have been carried out in close co-operation in order that the -- each of these formations would be well acquainted with the plans of the other and that incidents of friendly fire would be avoided. That is why co-ordination is done well ahead to clearly establish the responsibilities of all the parties during these operations. And, Your Honours, this can be found at page -- at the page of the transcript 11183. At transcript page 9815, Colonel Crosland - as he himself put it - based on his wealth of experience gained [Realtime transcript read in error "again"] across the world testified that it was quite expected that there should be various forms of co-ordination and co-operation between the forces of the MUP and VJ in Kosovo in order to, among other things, avoid friendly fire. This is transcript page 9815. In addition to these testimonies, we have the SFRY legislation in force at the time which General Lazarevic was duty-bound to adhere to which envisaged the engagement of Yugoslav Army units in operations against renegade terrorist groups. This was fully legitimate and legal. You can find this in Exhibit P1085. Your Honours, line 8, Colonel Crosland and his wealth of experience "gained" across the world; that is what the transcript should reflect. The evidence that we drew the attention of the Appellate Chamber to clearly shows that the planning and participation in the joint VJ-MUP operations in counter-terrorist actions is not only legitimate and customary but also necessary, especially in a situation where an armed force is attempting to separate a part of the territory of an internationally recognised country. The MUP and the VJ had an constitutional obligation to protect the territorial integrity and the sovereignty of the country. The Trial Chamber further found that the appellant demonstrated his actus reus also by issuing the orders of Grom 3 and Grom 4 as well as the Joint Command orders drafted by the Pristina Corps which sent the VJ into actions in those locations where there was forcible displacement of Albanians. At this point the Defence wishes to point out that the units of the Pristina Corps were deployed in all the various locations in Kosovo, including those where instances of deportation and forcible transfer were not found to have happened. The crucial issue is that the Chamber invoked those orders which clearly and unequivocally constituted a broader plan for the use of the Army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo and Metohija which had to do with the defence of the country from land aggression and a plan which had been drafted at a level higher than that of the Pristina Corps. The contents itself indicate that the plan was not erected against the civilian population but was rather the result of a war effort for the defence of the country. I will recall briefly something you can see in the slide. 3D690 is a directive of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 16th of January, 1999, which bears the heading Grom 3. This directive conveys the task to the lower levels, first the 3rd Army and then the Pristina Corps, to apply this use of VJ -- or, rather, to use VJ units in combat against forcible deployment of a multi-national NATO brigade and incursions of the terrorist units from Albania into Kosovo and Metohija. On the basis of this directive, the 3rd Army issued an order, Grom 3, on the 27th of January, 1999, in order to define the tasks of the Pristina Corps to prevent the deployment of a NATO brigade and its joining up with the KLA. This is 5D245. At the same time and further down the chain of command, this order, this plan for the defence of the country, was transformed by the 3rd Army command into an order to block and destroy the KLA in Drenica, Mlaka -- Laba, Malo Kosovo, and Malisevo. The 3rd Army sent out an order that the plan should be carried out at the latest by the 15th of February, 1999. This was 5D249. On the 16th of February the order was, in fact, carried out and issued to carry out these actions, and this is P2808. This was, in fact, an order that was then issued by the Pristina Corps command. The fact that this was all done to defend the country finds support also in a foreign intelligence report which is 60 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 6D1671 from November 1998 which follows the activities in the field. And I apologise, the number is 6D1671. This intelligence report which was sent through the embassy in Belgrade to the country in question discusses the activities and the organisation of the KLA, noting in particular that the KLA was being re-established and mobilised in Malisevo, Drenica, and Podujevo, that's to say Lab and Malo Kosovo, where some of the strongest and best organised KLA units were spotted. It was indicated that the KLA was actively recruiting and training new groups. Witness Radojko Stefanovic also testified, and at transcript page 21817 he stated that the 16th of February, 1999, order of the Pristina Corps stemmed from the order of the 3rd Army. And, therein, it was assessed that the areas of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo where there was a high concentration, a high presence, of the KLA units, these areas were suitable for an air-borne attack by a multi-national brigade of NATO. All this evidence which clearly corroborates the orders clearly lead to the conclusion that these were actions, orders undertaken for the purpose of the defence of the country, undertaken with the desire and with the goal of carrying out combat aims. With an analysis of all these orders we can establish what the objective of the actions of the VJ was and what the chain of command was. These were obviously orders for the defence of the country and there are no illegal orders or directions there. The appellant was obliged to carry out such orders from a superior command. The content of all of these orders and the corroborating evidence unequivocally lead to the conclusion that they do not constitute a screen or a mask in order to conceal that crimes were committed against Albanian civilian population under the guise of alleged fighting against the KLA and in defence of the NATO campaign. If that is not the only reasonable conclusion, then at least it is an alternative reasonable conclusion which should have been made by the Trial Chamber. I repeat, by issuing -- the issuance of these orders was taken by the Trial Chamber. One of the actus reus in the responsibility of General Lazarevic. In my view, when you analyse these orders the only reasonable conclusion would be that they were conducted for the purpose of the defence of the country and within war efforts. If you would like to lower the standards, in view of the fact that the Trial Chamber reasoned on the basis of circumstantial evidence, then at least a reasonable alternative conclusion is that these were orders that had to do with the war effort and defence. Especially when we're talking about the fact that in these places that the orders refer to, the KLA concentrations were exceptionally high and the members of the KLA were mixed in with the Albanian civilian population. The Trial Chamber -- the appellant would like to note that the Trial Chamber erroneously and without relying on specific evidence established that among other things Lazarevic demonstrated actus reus of aiding and abetting deportation and forcible transfer by going out into the field and touring the units, whereby he boosted the combat morale of the soldiers. The Defence would like to remind the Appeals Chamber that in the relevant period units of the VJ in Kosovo and Metohija were exposed to fierce bombing from the air and by frequent attacks of the KLA in the whole territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In such circumstances, it is absolutely logical for the corps commander to tour his units. This is done by every commander of any army in the world. The Trial Chamber does not have one direct and then we would say either an indirect proof that the tour of units was conducted with the awareness or intent to encourage and support the perpetrators of crimes. We repeat that in order for -- this is something that circumstantial evidence would need to point to in order for the conclusion of the Trial Chamber to be the only reasonable conclusion which would believe that that was not the case in this instance. Your Honours, you have the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in front of you, Your Honours, and in the position of the Defence this is exculpatory evidence. If you look at Exhibit P2004, Your Honours, you will see that item 4, dealing with the state of morale, General Lazarevic notifies the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff of the VJ of the following. This is a combat report of the 13th of April, 1999, some 20 days thus after the NATO campaign and the bombing began. General Lazarevic says the morale of the corps is very good and stable. The morale is positively influenced by the increasingly prominent view of international political factors, that the issue of Kosovo and Metohija should and must be dealt with by political means. And here is what the result is of Lazarevic's tour of the field. He's encouraging, he's reporting to the superior [as interpreted] 3rd command and the General Staff that the army in the field is prepared and in favour of a peaceful, political resolution of the situation. Would anyone who is aware of deportations and forcible transfer be in a position to report to the command that the awareness and morale of the soldiers is such that they wish for a political rather than a military resolution of the problem and that he would inform his superiors of such a position? What is particularly significant is also the testimony of Witness K73 who was mentioned the day before yesterday in the brief by my learned friend, Mr. Kremer, and also Mr. Ackerman referred to the testimony of this witness, Witness K73. My colleague, Mr. Cepic, talked about K90. I am now going to talk about the testimony of K73. My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, pointed to the testimony of this witness yesterday before the Trial Chamber and called or invited the Appeals Chamber to look at the testimony of this witness in detail. I would like the Chamber to review his testimony in detail so that you can see that even though this witness talked about an incident of deportation, he said that he never received an order for deportation or forcible transfer directly. When he testified, this witness talked about one incident here. My learned friend, Mr. Kremer, said the day before yesterday that this witness himself has a problem to face something that he allegedly himself did in one of the actions. But it is evident, however, that this witness does not recognise General Lazarevic as his co-perpetrator and aider and abettor in these acts. He recognises him as a commander; under his command he defended his country. And for him it was a great honour, as he himself said, to defend his country under the command of General Lazarevic. You will find this on T.341 [as interpreted] page of the transcript where Witness 73 says all officers had a high opinion about General Lazarevic. They held him to be a professional soldier, a good, honest, and honourable man who defended his country. He was one of a string of commanders or one in the chain of command of the commanders. The witness believed that Lazarevic was a military leader and emphasised that it was an exceptional honour for him to serve the homeland under his command. And finally, which of course is not the task of a witness but I would like to mention, this witness personally holds that General Lazarevic has no place in this courtroom. Your Honours, why am I talking about this? This is completely incompatible with the findings of the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber finds that General Lazarevic's tour in the field was such as to encourage and incite perpetrators of crimes, why then do the Prosecution witnesses, soldiers from the field, have an opinion like this of General Lazarevic? This is an absolute proof, actually, that General Lazarevic was thought to be a general leader in the defence of the country and that he did not have any influence or effect on any kind of illegal or ill deeds. This is transcript page "3415," Your Honours. This is an error in our transcript today. I am also going to mention Prosecution Witness Dusan Loncar who testified about General Lazarevic, said that he can state what most of the VJ officers believe and that is that he is a general par excellence. Prosecution Witness Zlatomir Pesic noted that he never received any order from General Lazarevic, either in writing or oral, that would oppose the law or basic rules on the use of the VJ. This is also a Prosecution witness. And finally, a witness, Prosecution, Ratomir Tanic gave an assessment that Lazarevic did not have a complete overview of what was happening on Kosovo and Metohija. The Trial Chamber -- this is transcript page 6756. Zlatomir Pesic is actually transcript page 7267; Dusan Loncar is transcript page 7687; and Ratomir Tanic is transcript page 6756. The Trial Chamber finally concludes erroneously that General Lazarevic knew that his failure to undertake adequate measures in order to ensure a proper investigation of serious crimes committed by the VJ enabled the forces to continue their terror of terror [as interpreted], violence, and transfer. The appellant notes that there is numerous evidence that the Trial Chamber did not evaluate correctly which indicate that General Lazarevic whenever he had knowledge of any crime by a member of the VJ carried out all measures at his disposal in order to investigate the crime and prosecute the perpetrators. There is numerous evidence which indicates without a reasonable doubt that -- there is extensive evidence proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that General Lazarevic failed to take appropriate measures to investigate serious crimes alleged committed by the VJ. I draw your attention to 5D84; that is Lazarevic's combat report of the 3rd of April, 1999. It's a report of the -- some seven or eight days after the beginning of the NATO bombing campaign. In this report General Lazarevic informs the superior command and the General Staff that the day before, on the 2nd of April, 32 criminal reports were brought against perpetrators of crimes and eight for murder, one for maltreatment, three for attempted murder, two for car theft, and so on and so forth. Thus, at the very beginning of the bombing campaign whenever General Lazarevic received information he would submit a report to the superior command and inform them about it. This exhibit was shown to General Vasiljevic, Prosecution witness. He was part of the intelligence organ in the General Staff of the VJ -- actually, the security organ - I apologise - at the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Vasiljevic, and I'm just going to summarise what he said - these are transcript pages 8965, 8966 - where he says that this is a classic example of a combat report as it should be drafted containing all the necessary elements. After that Witness Vasiljevic was shown Exhibit 5D85, a combat report of the 4th of April, 1999, the following day after the combat report of the 3rd of April where General Lazarevic regarding the security says the day before there was six criminal reports filed against perpetrators. Can we look at the following slide, please. And then again when General Vasiljevic was shown this document, General Vasiljevic - and you have that on this slide - replied that in this combat report as well -- this combat report as well contains everything that such a combat report should contain. He added -- he added that there was a duty by the security organ as well, that is, his line of reporting, to report back on these crimes. He also, when asked whether what General Lazarevic wrote -- what he wrote in the combat report and whether he undertook everything that he could and was able to do, he said yes, certainly. What General Lazarevic did was what he was supposed to do and his responsibility ended with that. Any further investigation was in the hands of higher organs and superior organs if required were obliged to request a more detailed report about these events. And you can find this on transcript 8967 to 8968. The said conduct by General Lazarevic which the Trial Chamber erroneously characterised as acts and omissions constituting the actus reus of aiding and abetting, deportations, and forcible transfer actually must be viewed exclusively as conduct directed at conducting war, or rather, behaviour which in real circumstances constitutes war efforts to defend the territory of a recognised state from armed rebellion and violent secession conducted by the KLA as well as for purposes of defence from the NATO air campaign. In view of all the evidence that we have noted, it is clear that a reasonable trier of fact can only necessarily come to such a decision. The Prosecution should have proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the acts and omissions by General Lazarevic which we cited above were specifically directed at providing practical assistance to perpetrators of crime and that these acts had a significant effect on the execution of crimes. In a case in which such a conclusion is based on circumstantial evidence, this should have been the only reasonable conclusion that could have been drawn from such evidence. It's evident that the examples that we cited as well as other numerous examples from our appeal brief do not allow the Trial Chamber the option to establish that the only reasonable conclusion was that General Lazarevic had the requisite actus reus through the above-cited conduct and alleged omissions. The alternative reasonable explanation of Lazarevic's conduct would be in taking legal measures directed at conducting war and defence of the country and not to perpetrator of crimes. In light of the latest jurisprudence, the Defence believes that in this specific case General Lazarevic -- we would need to apply to him the principle of specific direction, regardless of the fact that at the relevant time he was in Kosovo where allegedly deportations and forcible transfers were taking place. The entire territory of Kosovo cannot be considered as one crime scene, especially if we keep in mind the circumstances of daily mass and wide spread bombing on the part of the NATO Alliance and practically daily attacks of the KLA against units of the VJ and MUP. Due to these specific circumstances it was necessary to establish whether General Lazarevic was present at each specific place where a crime was committed. Had General Lazarevic reacted when he knew of any crime or when he found out about any crime, this is indicated by the following examples that he did react: 5D379 is General Lazarevic's request of the 26th of April, 1999, when he asked the superior organs to send urgently to Kosovo a forensic expert team in order to exhume bodies because of alleged information that the Army of Yugoslavia was implicated in crimes and killings in Mali Alas. Also, if you look at Exhibit 5D383 you will see that immediately the following day, the VMA sent Dr. Ivica Milosavljevic to help in the investigation of these crimes. What is of particular interest - and I would like to draw the attention of the Chamber to that - is the following: PD383 [as interpreted]. This is what it says, that a forensic expert, or rather, a military expert, a pathologist, will carry out exhumations throughout the territory of the Pristina Corps for as long as necessary. So this is not a call in respect of one particular situation or crime. This is a call for this forensic pathologist to remain in Kosovo, to deal with the entire area of Kosovo, and to stay for as long as necessary. A few days later, that is to say at the beginning of May -- previously, Your Honours, I do apologise, I would like to draw your attention to the following: PD1315 [as interpreted]. And that is a report, a forensic report, of Dr. Milosavljevic in terms of what he did at Mali Alas and Slovinje. Number 1, this report shows that the call was not just mere writing on paper. Something that was just supposed to show that General Lazarevic did something. It was a sincere, meaningful call to investigate the situation and to punish the possible perpetrators. As for 5D1315, the report on the forensic examination of bodies at these two locations shows that this was truly done. Further on, 5D421 shows that precisely on the basis of this evidence that was initiated by General Lazarevic UNMIK prosecuted crimes at these particular locations. I would like to draw your attention to 5D421 which shows that immediately after that, on the 8th of May, 1999, General Lazarevic once again sent a letter to the superior command requesting two more teams of pathologists, forensic pathologists, to carry out additional examinations. Please do focus on this document. General Lazarevic says that all these pathologists are going to perform their functions according to the orders issued by the military court. This shows that he has no further authority with regard to these matters. In view of such situations and in view of clear evidence that in each and every case when he was aware of the commission of any crime, General Lazarevic took adequate measures and appropriate measures, the only ones he could have taken. It is quite clear that because of this specific situation of a war, that is to say lack of sufficient information, the impossibility of observing things directly, it was necessary for the Trial Chamber to deal with each and every location of forcible deportation to see whether General Lazarevic was actually there or close to that location or whether he knew that specifically at these locations members of the VJ conducted deportations or forcible transfers. Therefore, we believe that in the case when General Lazarevic was commander of the Pristina Corps the principle of specific direction has to be applied in this case as well, and it has to be established whether General Lazarevic was present at each and one of these locations of deportation or whether he was close to any one of them and whether he could have known that soldiers under his command could have carried out such deportations. I would also like to recall the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. I'd like to go back to something else. I do apologise to the Trial Chamber, but I'm trying to fit into the time allocated to me. So I would like to say that General Gojovic, who was a Defence witness, said that military judicial organs dealt with 601 victims at 11 locations; 16687 is the transcript reference. Also Defence Witness Geza Farkas said that when at the General Staff they recapitulated the situation, their assessment was that at Kosovo and Metohija, at the relevant point in time, 95 per cent of crimes that were believed to have been committed by members of the VJ were criminally prosecuted. Also I would like to draw your attention to 5D550, the commander of the 175th Brigade of the VJ, I'm saying that criminal reports were filed, although the Trial Chamber says something different. As for Witness Geza Farkas, 16304 is the transcript page reference. Your Honours -- actually, when you assess all this evidence, with all due respect, I would like to remind you of something that of course you know full well. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal does say that presence alone at the scene of a crime is not conclusive of aiding and abetting unless it is shown to have a significant legitimatising or encouraging effect on the principal perpetrator, and so on; this is the Boskoski and Tarculovski trial judgement, paragraph 402, and Brdjanin appeal judgement, paragraph 273, 277. Therefore, I believe it is absolutely necessary here to establish specific direction of General Lazarevic in terms of aiding and abetting in forcible transfers and deportations as far as actus reus is concerned. Also I would like to add something else. Prosecutor versus Perisic, that is another case I would like to deal with. General assistance provided cannot be sufficient evidence in terms of crimes committed by direct perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the actual text of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, it is necessary to establish a direct link between the immediate perpetrator. In these cases of actus reus that was established by the Trial Chamber in relation to General Lazarevic, we see no such thing. This can be found in the appeals judgement of Perisic in paragraph 44. In the evidence of this case there is not a shred of evidence that would indicate any direct link of General Lazarevic in the aforementioned case. Also, in the Perisic case it was stated that awareness of the commission of a crime does not establish, per se, specific direction consisting of actus reus separate from mens rea. That can be seen in paragraph 68 of the same judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the interpreter's note. Yes, we are going to submit the original text of these judgements to the interpreters. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to move on to questions related to the following, whether the standard of mens rea was met in terms of aiding and abetting in the case of General Lazarevic. Perhaps at this point in time it would be right for me to try to respond to the question put by the honourable Appeals Chamber to deal with the following question: Actus reus and mens rea in terms of aiding and abetting as part of joint criminal enterprise, whether that can be in existence before the JCE itself. The Defence believes that that's not possible, that that cannot be achieved in such a way. In my modest view as Defence counsel, for as long as there is not an objective the accused cannot assist in carrying out crimes that are within this joint purpose. Before the joint enterprise or joint objective or joint purpose comes into being, it is not possible to achieve actus reus and not mens rea either. An aider and abettor has to be aware of crimes and also to know that his conduct significantly contributes to the commission of such crimes. However, an aider and abettor does not accept a possible plan or objective of the enterprise as his own, and in this particular case I'm claiming that he's not even aware of one and does not share this common purpose with the others. That's why I believe that actus reus and mens rea before this plan started at all cannot pertain to deportations and forcible transfers before this plan had been embarked upon. If you believe that this would suffice, then I would like to move on. Thank you, Your Honours. The Trial Chamber erred in determining that the appellant had the necessary mens rea for the crimes of aiding and abetting and the deportation and forcible transfer of Albanian civilians because he was aware of the intentional commission of such crimes by the VJ in co-ordinated actions with the MUP and he knew that his conduct assisted the commission of these crimes. This is paragraph 927 of the trial judgement. Before the Defence starts dealing with the evidence that shows on the contrary, beyond any reasonable doubt, that General Lazarevic was not aware of any kind of intentional commission of these crimes and he did not know that his conduct assisted the commission of these crimes, we wish to point out now that in this specific case and in view of the aforementioned specific characteristics of this concrete case, in the view of this Defence a standard has to be applied that implies the existence of a purpose or an objective. Article 25(3)(c) of the Rome Statute. Why am I saying in this specific case and in view of the specific circumstances involved? The NATO air campaign and the alleged simultaneous start of crimes of deportation and forcible transfers under the guise of this campaign as well as previously mentioned evidence make it necessary to adjust the criterion for assessment to these circumstances. This simply is not sufficient. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber had to determine that the appellant acted with an objective in mind of committing such crimes because knowledge is not sufficient for the existence -- responsibility according to this. However, on the other hand, if this kind of position taken by the Defence is not to be accepted, again the accused has to know that his action or failure to act would assist the main perpetrators of certain crimes. He would have to know that at least some of these crimes would be committed. This is a standard that is also higher than had reason to know. In addition to that, the Defence believes that every professional soldier and even a lay person knows that in any war there is a risk that individuals may commit crimes against the civilian population that cannot be prevented. Therefore, the Defence believes that when the NATO campaign started the Trial Chamber had to establish beyond reasonable doubt that this kind of knowledge did exist on the basis of specific evidence related to this accused. Even if some information about deportations and forcible transfers carried out by members of the VJ had been generally known and widely disseminated, this would not support a presumption of the knowledge of the accused, in this case General Lazarevic. The Trial Chamber erred in finding that Lazarevic knew that through his conduct he would help further the campaign of the forcible displacement of Kosovo Albanians. The Defence did not manage to identify the piece of evidence that the Trial Chamber relied upon and which would show beyond reasonable doubt that Lazarevic knew that he would further this campaign through his conduct. If Lazarevic was aware of it and even if he knew that the Kosovo Albanians were leaving the province, there is no evidence that would show beyond reasonable doubt that Lazarevic was aware that this was the result of the force used by his subordinates, especially not -- and there is especially no evidence showing beyond reasonable doubt that Lazarevic knew that with his conduct he was assisting a campaign of forcible displacement and deportations. It is to be noted that as the first NATO bombs landed there were many Serbian civilians who were leaving the area as well. Your Honours, I don't know if this is the right time based on your guidance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. And we'll take a break for 30 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we took the break, Your Honours, I gave my modest view with regard to the mens rea of General Lazarevic. In an attempt to support my view, I would first like you to -- to point you to Volume III, paragraph 906, of the trial judgement -- or actually, paragraphs 901 through 906, where the findings are related about the measures that General Lazarevic took. The Defence believes that the findings of the Trial Chamber which can be found at paragraph 906 where it is stated that General Lazarevic took measures to help the civilian population but that this showed that he was aware of the forcible displacement of the Kosovo Albanians by the VJ forces and that these orders also show that he tried to carry these actions out in a non-violent manner and not with the intention to displace the civilians. I would like to draw your attention to some of these orders, P2029, on the 1st of April, this is six days after the bombing. The order said that measures of prevention are to be applied, prevent looting and other forms of crime. Evidently at the very start of bombing as an experienced officer General Lazarevic issued orders with the intention of preventing crimes, seeking to have the civilians protected from every form of theft and other criminal offences. This is quite understandable, and in our view this does not go to show that he knew that these acts were being committed or that they were being committed systematically or in an organised fashion. Rather, this was a war where NATO bombs were destroying the residences and businesses of citizens and where such occurrences were a possibility. The other order, P1306, directly contradicts - and quite clearly so - the finding by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 906. If you look at the order dated the 16th of April, 1999, you will see that General Lazarevic stated the following: "Because of the NATO forces' activity and the activities of SDS's on -- against the civilian population, the corps forces were under daily attack and directly threatened. In order to avert losses among the civilian population from the activities of the aggressor, I hereby issue the following order ..." And what follows is the order that at all the various levels of the corps, regardless of the location - since the Trial Chamber said that these orders were related to those areas where the crime of deportation occurred - here we see that all the corps units were instructed to set out special elements of their forces that would be solely concerned with the protection of the civilian population. Therefore, from the preamble of this order we can infer the knowledge of General Lazarevic. He saw the movement of the civilian population as the result of the attack of the air forces and the attack of the terrorist forces against the VJ and MUP forces. I would also like to draw your attention to Exhibit P -- to Exhibit 5D201 dated the 1st of April, 1999. I apologise, Your Honour, my mistake. 5D201 dated the 19th of April, 1999. The heading also reads "signed personally by General Vladimir Lazarevic, commander." In view of the air raids by NATO or as a result of the air raids by NATO, the civilian population within the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps has started moving and I hereby order, so the reason behind the order is clearly stated. All the corps units should see what the situation is with regard to the civilian population on the move, and wherever possible protect the civilian population and prevent any movement and spilling. Therefore, General Lazarevic clearly said what his understanding of the reasons why the civilian population on -- were on the move was, states the air raids as the reasons. He clearly asks from his personnel to find relevant facilities, to set out the forces, and these forces that were sent out to protect the civilian population should provide the protection indeed, and, as it is stated here, prevent any movement and spilling. Therefore, General Lazarevic ordered that any deportation or forcible transfer be prevented. Likewise, in Exhibit 5D372 on the 22nd of April, that's to say less than a month after the start of bombing, General Lazarevic gave an assessment that it was on account of NATO raids and a terrorist activity that the civilian population was on the move. Under 3, he states in this order: "Speed up the return of civilians who are returning to the villages and towns from where they were moved out. Do not allow civilian refugee groups to remain in the areas of defence of the brigades. Ensure a safe return of refugees to the places that they left previously." So this clearly shows an instance where General Lazarevic is asking from his subordinates that all those persons who left their homes, as we saw earlier on, because of NATO bombing and terrorist activities, be allowed to and enabled to return home. Is this a clear showing that General Lazarevic was aware of deportations and forcible transfer and that he was indeed making a significant contribution to such acts? Please look at 5D370 as well, where on the 23rd of April, a day after the earlier order of the 22nd April, General Lazarevic ordered under 3: "Accommodate the population in keeping with the already issued orders of the command of the Pristina Corps. The population should be put up in the settlements and ensure that it is controlled. Prevent any misconduct especially in the lower command structure with regard to the civilian population." Those held responsible for this task, brigade commanders. This is 5D374. Your Honour, Your Honours, we have provided numerous such examples in our appeals brief, and this isn't the time to reiterate them nor is it allowed. We just wanted to draw your attention to some of them. You will find all the other orders in our brief and, more importantly, you will find the reports which show that the subordinate units reported to the General on the activities taken, which goes to show that this was not just a piece of paper; rather, this was an attempt to protect the civilian population in a state of war and that this was the actual intention and wish on the part of General Lazarevic. Your Honour, Your Honours, I believe I still have four or five minutes left. I'd like to address now the third question that you put, respectfully. The question was to discuss whether and under what circumstances the mens rea of aiding and abetting, deportation, and other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes other than deportation and other inhumane acts. In our appeals brief, we have already stated the position of the Defence about the knowledge of General Lazarevic of the crimes that the VJ forces committed in 1998. We gave numerous examples showing that from the presence of foreign observers, whether the KDOM or the KVM, there were different views as to what the conduct of the VJ forces was. The Defence holds that - and this is a humble answer to your question - that when it comes to the alleged crimes committed in 1998 and those committed in 1999, they are not identical in essentials. And since there is no essential identity between these two, any possible knowledge of the crimes in 1998 would, in our view, have no substantial effect on the mens rea of aiding and abetting, deportation, and other inhumane acts. In this particular case we had occasion to hear, although quite unjustly, we didn't have an opportunity to adduce evidence on this, that the -- these VJ activities in 1998 were in August and September. After the October Agreement, foreign observers arrived. And since that point, up until the start of NATO bombing on the 24th of March, 1999, there were no combat activities. If there was an incident, it was sporadic, save for perhaps one or two incidents. There was a very important interruption in the sequence of events, in our view. Now, since there are factors which interrupt the chain of events, they support the conclusion that there should also be an interruption in the natural sequence of consequences. If this notion of direction is implied in the finding about the existence of substantial assistance, then there must also exist a connection between actions and crimes that the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt. Because there is such an interruption in the chain of events, under no circumstances can a finding be made that the mens rea of aiding and abetting, deportation, and forcible transfer can be inferred from the events that transpired in 1998. In 1998 there was allegedly excessive use of force, and in 1998 we had the internally displaced persons. There were no deportations or forcible transfers. We talk about internally displaced persons in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, one thing, I would like to seek your clarification. On the transcript, 42 , 17, it says, "They are identical in essentials." I wonder whether it should be, "They are not identical in essentials"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are not. They are not identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you are out of our time allocated to you, but I give you one minute to finish your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I'm certainly not a better lawyer than Mr. Ackerman, but I am certainly much poorer timekeeper. If you will allow me that one minute to say that our Defence is convinced that in the sea of evidence that we have presented, you will discern the errors the Trial Chamber made in their factual and legal findings that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. I'm sure that the Appeals Chamber will do that and that General Lazarevic will live to see justice done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It seems to me there's no questions from the Bench. Now we would like to hear the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, General Lazarevic was one of the most important linchpins for the implementation of the common criminal purpose. As the highest tactical commander of the large VJ force in Kosovo, General Lazarevic's assistance and support was required to plan joint VJ-MUP operations and deploy VJ troops and equipment on the ground. Lazarevic acted with Pavkovic, the 3rd Army commander, and others to plan and co-ordinate joint operations through which the campaign of forcible expulsions in Kosovo was unleashed. In pursuit of this planning and General Lazarevic's Joint Command orders, VJ troops using VJ weaponry and resources systematically and brutally expelled more than 700.000 Kosovo Albanians from their homes over the border to Albania in little over three months. As the campaign of terror unfolded, Lazarevic's troops reported back up the chain of command that operations had gone according to plan and he himself reported upwards to Pavkovic in the 3rd Army. Despite his intimate and protracted involvement in the operations that targeted the Kosovo Albanian population, the Trial Chamber rendered a very cautious conviction of Lazarevic for aiding and abetting forcible displacements by his VJ forces that was based on a careful and detailed consideration of the totality of the evidence in the case. Lazarevic has shown no error in these cautious findings and his appeal should be dismissed. I should perhaps just be clear and say that it is the Prosecution's position that some of the Trial Chamber's findings, in fact, were too cautious as will be discussed by my colleagues on Friday. Your Honours, to give a road map to you for what I'm going to be saying this morning, first, I will explain why General Lazarevic's appeal should be dismissed; second, I will respond to Your Honours' questions which we have labelled questions five, six, and seven; and third, I will turn to the issues arising from the Perisic appeals judgement. I expect to be about an hour and a half so there should be room for questions whenever Your Honours wish to. Now, first, turning to General Lazarevic's appeal and why it should be dismissed. Most of General Lazarevic's appeal is simply a cut and paste from his final trial brief. His appeal essentially boils down to his disagreement with and different evaluation of the evidence from the Trial Chamber's assessment of evidence in the case. He fails to show any errors in the judgement; that is to say, he fails to show that the assessment was unreasonable and occasioned a miscarriage of justice. He has failed to meet the standard of review. Your Honours, General Lazarevic's argument fall into a number of categories that we have discussed in our response brief and I'm not going to go into that again here, but one category is, as I mentioned, mere repeats of submissions made at trial. I would also like to point out that my learned colleagues do not make reference correctly to the Trial Chamber's findings and the use of evidence needs to be closely scrutinised. At page 6, for example, submissions were made regarding the Srbica events and it was stated that the evidence showed and the findings were in the judgement that there was a whole range of exculpatory reports. But, Your Honours, the events that are being discussed in the judgement took place in March. If Your Honours look at the exhibits that were referred to by the Defence, they all are reports from a month later, from the 20th of April, from the 3rd, 5th, and 16th of May, so they have absolutely no bearing on the Trial Chamber's findings about what happened in March. And, Your Honours, there are also issues about how the Trial Chamber's findings are being presented. Today at transcript page 38, there's a discussion -- there was a discussion of paragraph 906 of the judgement. It was said that it was found by the Trial Chamber that General Lazarevic had no intention to displace the civilians. It was being said as if that was a finding in that paragraph. It is not. That paragraph actually says that he did have the intent but that there was also evidence that he was trying to make efforts to ensure it was done in a non-violent way which is completely different. The finding was that he had intent to displace, but as we know from the judgement there was no sufficient evidence to convict him of other crimes. We'll get back to some of that on Friday. So, Your Honours, we submit as we did in the Prosecution's response brief, that General Lazarevic's appeal should be summarily dismissed on the basis of the consistent jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber in Krajisnik, Martic, Strugar, and Brdjanin. That leads me to addressing Your Honours' fifth question. Your Honours have asked the parties to address with reference to the Trial Chamber's findings whether a breach of duty imposed by national, military, disciplinary law may amount to aiding and abetting by omission under customary international law. Your Honours, we submit that in this case it is actually not necessary for the Appeals Chamber to determine whether a duty imposed by national military disciplinary law alone may amount to aiding and abetting by omission under customary international law. The duty of a commander to prevent or punish violations of international humanitarian law by his subordinate is one of the most fundamental duties imposed by the laws and customs of war. The ICRC study on customary international humanitarian law calls it "a long-standing rule of customary international law." And that is ICRC study -- yes, ICRC study rule 153. The duty is encapsulated in the provisions of Additional Protocol I, Articles 86 and 87, but was used as the basis for conviction of commanders following the Second World War in the High Command Case and the Yamashita case. It is also recognised in the ICTY case law as an international duty under which criminal liability under Article 7(1) could arise for a breach; for example, in the Blaskic appeals judgement, paragraphs 663 and 664. Aiding and abetting by omission based on a breach of duty in international law is not in question. That's found in the Mrksic appeal judgement at paragraph 151. The Trial Chamber recognised that a commander's duty to prevent or punish crimes by his subordinates can arise to 7(1) liability at Volume I, paragraph 90, and Volume III, paragraph 622. In addition, when discussing Article 7(3), the Chamber stated that: "The duty to prevent and the duty to punish are distinct and separate responsibilities under international law, and an omission to carry out either duty may give rise to its own charges in an indictment."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the counsel to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My apologies. This is found in Volume I, paragraph 116, and I refer Your Honours also to the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement, paragraph 259, and the Blaskic appeal judgement, paragraph 83. While the Trial Chamber explored national military justice laws and regulations, this was relevant evidence of Lazarevic's material ability to act and the types of measures that were open to him in his position to prevent crimes and punish crimes by his subordinates. And this analysis is found in Volume I, paragraph 518 to 523. These national laws reflected and incorporated commanders' duties under international law. Unless Your Honours have questions, I will move to the next question. Thank you. Turning to -- now to your sixth question which asks the parties to discuss as a legal matter as well as with respect to the particular Trial Chamber's findings whether the actus reus and mens rea of aiding and abetting that formed part of the JCE may be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the JCE. Your Honours, as a matter of law, the timing of the existence of the common purpose in this case is irrelevant to General Lazarevic's conviction for aiding and abetting. Under our law the aider and abettor has to contribute to the commission of the crime, not to the joint criminal enterprise. That's found in Kvocka appeals judgement, paragraph 91. It is well established in the jurisprudence that aiding and abetting can take place before, during, and after a crime occurs. And I refer, Your Honours, for example, to the Nahimana appeals judgement, paragraph 482; and the Blagojevic and Jokic appeals judgement, paragraph 127; Simic appeals judgement, paragraph 85; and the Blaskic appeals judgement, paragraph 48. Now, in this case crimes of forcible displacement were committed between March and June 1999, as set out in detail in Volume I. The crimes were committed both by the JCE members but also by the physical perpetrators who were found to have the intent to deport. There's specific findings at the end of each section dealing with the different crime bases about the perpetrators' intent. I'll just refer Your Honours to the general findings in Volume III, paragraph 92 and 95. If Your Honours wish, I can also provide references to all the paragraphs in Volume II, but it may not be necessary. Thank you. However, neither the identity of the perpetrators nor whether they shared the intent with someone else, i.e., they formed a JCE, is relevant for aiding and abetting. Indeed "a defendant may be convicted of having aided and abetted a crime even if the principal perpetrators have not been ... identified." That's found in the Brdjanin appeal judgement, paragraph 355; and the Krstic appeal judgement, paragraph 143. The coincidence of General Lazarevic's actus reus and mens rea occurred before and during the commission of deportations in 1999. General Lazarevic was aware that crimes of forcible displacement were probably going to be committed by VJ forces and he knowingly provided assistance to the commission of these crimes. His assistance substantially contributed to the forcible displacement crimes for which he was convicted. That is all that is required for him to be held responsible as an aider and abettor. And this brings me, unless there are questions, to question number seven. Question number seven asked whether and under what circumstances the mens rea of aiding and abetting deportation and forcible transfer may be inferred from the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including other crimes than deportation and forcible transfer. In short, Your Honours, the Prosecution's position is that yes, Lazarevic 's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998 is relevant in establishing his mens rea for aiding and abetting crimes that occurred in 1999. My colleague, Ms. Monchy, has already provided Your Honours with the legal basis for such an approach. And indeed, it is common and quite proper use of evidence adopted and approved by many Trial and Appeals Chambers at this Tribunal. As a matter of law, there are no specific circumstances in which this is not allowed. It is ultimately a factual or evidentiary question. I will therefore just address Your Honours on the facts of this case relating to General Lazarevic.
