General Lazarevic's knowledge of the massive forcible displacements in 1999 -- excuse me, 1998, is directly relevant to his knowledge of the substantial likelihood that the same crimes being committed during 1999. In addition, the nature of some of the other crimes such as arson and murder as well as the scale of them in 1998 is also relevant to his knowledge of the substantial likelihood of forcible displacements in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is kindly asked to take into account interpretation and slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do apologise once again. Your Honours have heard about the many sources of knowledge of the 1998 crimes from my colleagues already this week. I will, a bit later, distribute a bundle of material where we will be referring to some specific material in the bundle we have prepared, and in that bundle you will find some charts similar to the ones you have been given yesterday. Since I don't propose to go through those charts specifically -- I see your colleague is handing them out. Okay, let's hand them out now. Your Honours, my -- I'm sorry. I can see Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections from the defendants for us to have this bundle of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless that is being admitted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And thank you to my learned colleagues. Your Honours, in this bundle there are two -- there are two tables: One set out the source of General Lazarevic's knowledge of crimes in 1998 and the other table sets out the sources of knowledge in 1999. I'm afraid there's a typo on the front page of the overview, but I think it's self explanatory. As I said, I'm not intending to go through this in any detail today as all of these sources have been discussed so exhaustively already during the proceedings in this appeal. Of course, if there are questions I'm happy to address them. But what all of this shows is that General Lazarevic knew of a broad range of crimes such as looting, arson, and murder which were committed repeatedly by the VJ and the MUP against Kosovo Albanians in 1998. In addition, Lazarevic was informed of the massive flight of civilians that resulted from these crimes and the heavy-handed tactics used by joint VJ-MUP forces. It was with this knowledge that General Lazarevic became the commander of the Pristina Corps in 1999. Knowing that his VJ forces had frequently violated -- sorry, had frequently committed violent crimes that had resulted in massive forcible displacements of Kosovo Albanians, he knew that there was a substantial likelihood that these same troops acting in similar joint operations with the MUP would continue to use the same heavy-handed tactics and extreme violence against the Kosovo Albanian population and that the Kosovo Albanians would be forced to flee as a result. The Trial Chamber reasonably held that in 1999 General Lazarevic was "aware that similar excessive use of force and forcible displacements were likely to occur if he ordered the VJ to operate in Kosovo in 1999." Volume III, paragraph 923. So on the facts of this case, Lazarevic's knowledge of crimes in 1998 included deportations and forcible transfer and was directly relevant to the same crimes being committed in 1999. However, the Prosecution submits that if General Lazarevic knew from the events in 1998 that VJ forces would probably commit widespread crimes, including looting and burning of homes, and inflict extreme violence on civilians in 1999, then he would also have known that the civilian population would probably be forced to flee in order to escape this. Therefore, his knowledge of widespread crimes including violence was relevant to his knowledge of the probability of forced displacement. And finally, I would like to stress that the Trial Chamber's findings on General Lazarevic's knowledge in 1998 was just one of many strands which enabled -- which established his knowledge and his mens rea for aiding and abetting during events in 1999. This is illustrated by the second table that I discussed at the beginning of my answer to Your Honours' question. Again, I'm not suggesting that we necessarily need to look at it today. I would like at the end of my submission on question seven to note that I got the impression that my learned friends were arguing a new ground of appeal today. It was said that the Rome Statute of the ICC had a purpose standard for aiding and abetting and that that purpose standard should be applied by this Appeals Chamber in this case. Your Honours, first of all, the mens rea standard of this Tribunal is clear. The standard is knowledge of a substantial likelihood. It is not a purpose standard. And secondly, the Rome Statute is not binding on the ICTY and is not necessarily a reflection of customary international law, and we would submit actually on this point it is not. We would refer Your Honours to the Katanga and Ngudjolo confirmation decision, paragraphs 507 and 508 regarding the binding nature of the ICC Statute and also to the ICC Statute Article 10. Your Honours, this includes -- unless I may further assist in relation to Your Honours' questions the Prosecution's response to the three questions that were put. No. Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I now turn to address the Perisic appeal judgement. First, I will show that there are cogent reasons for the Appeals Chamber to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement and specifically its findings on specific direction. And second, I will submit that if the Appeals Chamber does not find cogent reasons, then General Lazarevic's conviction should not be disturbed because of the Perisic appeal judgement. Turning to the first point on cogent reasons. There are four important cogent reasons to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement on specific direction. First, the Perisic appeal judgement has created a new specific direction element for aiding and abetting which is not found in customary international law. Second, the Perisic appeal judgement incorrectly interprets the Appeals Chamber's consistent jurisprudence. Third, it introduces vague concepts which lead to considerable uncertainties and difficulties in practice. And fourth, it undermines the respect for international humanitarian law and is against the interests of international justice. First, customary international law does not require specific direction as an element for aiding and abetting. I will not embark on a full exploration of customary international law today; that is not necessary. It was already done by this Tribunal 15 years ago. Customary international law on aiding and abetting was thoroughly examined in the Furundzija trial judgement. In a 20-page analysis of relevant international instruments and jurisprudence, the Furundzija trial judgement concluded that the mens rea of aiding and abetting according to customary international law is knowledge. And it held that "the actus reus of aiding and abetting in international criminal law requires practical assistance, encouragement, or moral support which has a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime." Furundzija trial judgement paragraphs 249 and 235. And there's no mention of any specific direction requirement. Only seven months later the Furundzija Trial Chamber -- sorry, I start that again. Only seven months after the Furundzija trial judgement, the Appeals Chamber rendered its judgement in the Tadic case. It contained no analysis of or reference to customary international law on aiding and abetting. And it is in that judgement that the wording "specific direction" appears for the first time in the Tribunal's jurisprudence. And it appears -- in the context in which it appears it indicates that the Appeals Chamber did not want to add a new element to aiding and abetting and this can be seen in the Tadic appeal judgement paragraph 229(iii). Specific direction was used only to explain some distinctions between aiding and abetting and joint criminal enterprise and not to add a new element. The Appeals Chamber did not explain where the wording "specific direction" came from; it provided no reasons as to why such a requirement is needed. It surely would have done so if it had intended to change or give guidance on the meaning of the Furundzija elements. Moreover, Your Honours, the conclusions of the Furundzija Trial Chamber were explicitly approved by the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski appeal judgement at paragraph 162. As we will return to later, it is also clear from the Aleksovski appeal -- of the -- sorry. It is also clear from the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber's explanation of the Tadic appeal judgement that it did not understand it as containing a "specific direction" element for aiding and abetting. None of the subsequent judgements that have reproduced the Tadic language discusses customary international law on the basis of specific direction as a requirement. It is therefore clear that customary international law, as authoritatively interpreted by the Tribunal, do not require specific direction for aiding and abetting liability, neither on the actus reus nor on the mens rea side. I would note as an aside here that the Perisic Appeals Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask you for your assistance. You said none of the subsequent judgements have reproduced the Tadic language discuss -- discussed international law on the basis of specific direction as a requirement. Can you mention these judgements if you have the references? What judgements are you referring to exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- when you mentioned the judgements that have reproduced the Tadic language?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: They are referred to in footnote 100 of the Perisic appeal judgement, but there are numerous judgements which have listed -- have lifted, if you like, the language of Tadic in setting out what the elements of aiding and abetting are. But none of them have had a discussion of -- it's a -- if I may, for consistency there have been a repetition of the very wording but there have never been a new interpretation of the language. That was the point I was trying to make. And we will provide you with a list of the cases if Your Honours will allow my colleague to compare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- if I may come back to this with a list of the specific case references I will do that in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So your point is that the only judgement that discusses that and gives an interpretation is Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel, I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you claim that specific direction is not an element for the aiding and abetting, how could you distinguish the law force support to a legitimate military action with the aiding and abetting of the criminal acts? Do you think the existing elements of the aiding and abetting is enough for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I will be addressing this at the very end as the fourth cogent reason. But in sum, Your Honour, we submit that it cannot be a question of the position of the specific perpetrator or the specific factual scenario which by the legal analysis of the elements of aiding and abetting. There's one set of elements for aiding and abetting that apply to everyone and ultimately it would be a factual determination whether assistance from one military organisation to another or whatever the factual scenario is, whether the elements of aiding and abetting are met based on the knowledge and substantial contribution standards that we have in the Tribunal. I don't know if that answers Your Honour's question. Thank you, Your Honour. So what I want to mention as an aside is that in the Perisic Appeals Chamber's judgement when it discusses the development of the jurisprudence on aiding and abetting, there's actually no reference neither to the Tadic -- sorry, neither to the Furundzija trial judgement nor to the endorsement of that judgement in the Furundzija appeal judgement -- I'm sorry, to the Furundzija trial judgement or the Aleksovski appeal judgement it should have been. Your Honours, the Perisic appeal judgement does not discuss customary international law except for one reference in footnote 115 to one World War II case, Zyklon B, which it incorrectly represents as supporting specific direction. It describes the case as "finding two defendants guilty of assisting crimes [sic] of concentration camp detainees by providing gas, despite arguments that the gas was to be used for lawful purposes ...," and then, "... after reviewing evidence that the defendants arranged for S.S. units to be trained in the use of this gas to kill humans." Your Honours, I respectfully submit that there is no way that the Zyklon B case can be interpreted in this way. And if I may refer to the handout that I provided Your Honours this morning. We have included an excerpt of the Zyklon B case, and I would invite Your Honours to look at this case with me. I would first like to draw Your Honours' attention to page 100 of the case which is on the second page of this little bundle. Your Honours will see how the Prosecution presented the case in its closing arguments. The essential parts I'm going to go through are numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. First the Prosecution said that the essential question was whether the accused knew of the purpose to which that gas was being put. Later on this report explains that: "Counsel said that it was unbelievable that Dr. Tesch did not know that anything wrong went on in the concentration camps." Again, clearly knowledge. The Prosecution also said that: "It was ... unbelievable that Dr. Tesch had no knowledge of the amount of gas being supplied to the S.S. and to Auschwitz in particular by a firm which was wholly his property." But also when the Judge Advocate summed up the case, the Judge Advocate at the passage that I've marked with a number 4 said that there were three facts which had to be considered. And the third fact was -- as I said: "Thirdly, the accused knew that the gas was to be used for the purpose of killing human beings." It is true that in the case there was some evidence of training, but that evidence was discussed in the judgement at paragraph -- at page 95 and the Defence contested this evidence and the Prosecution, as we can see, did not rely on it. I haven't included these passages but it's at pages 95, 97, and 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This interpretation by the Perisic appeal judgement of Zyklon B is all the more astonishing in that the Zyklon B case is discussed in quite some detail in the Furundzija trial judgement in paragraphs 222 and 223, which is a judgement which was approved by the Aleksovski appeal judgement. So, Your Honours, the Tribunal was created to prosecute those most responsible for serious international crimes under customary international law. In customary international law, there is no specific direction element either in the actus reus or on the mens rea elements of aiding and abetting. The Perisic appeal judgement, therefore, has departed from customary international law, which the Tribunal was created to apply. This in itself is a cogent reason for the Appeals Chamber to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement. And before I move on, if I may just return to Judge Pocar's question, the cases on specific direction can be found in the Perisic appeal judgement in footnote 70 and not footnote 100 as I incorrectly stated. I apologise for that. The second cogent reason to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement is that it ignores and misrepresents the Appeals Chamber's previous judgements which have explicitly rejected the specific direction element. First, the Furundzija appeal judgement completely ignores, as I've mentioned -- I'm sorry, I keep making the same mistake, it seems. First, the Perisic appeal judgement completely ignores the Furundzija trial judgement and the Aleksovski appeals judgement determination which limited the Tadic specific direction wording to its context. Your Honours, this -- there's an analysis found in -- of this in paragraphs 162 to 164 of the Aleksovski appeal judgement which makes this point, and I'll try to go through that in some detail now. In paragraph 162, the Aleksovski appeal judgement endorses the Furundzija trial judgement's statement of the elements of aiding and abetting which was the knowledge standard and the substantial contribution standard. And then it explains Tadic in paragraph 163, which Your Honours have on the screen now. It's a complicated paragraph, but it is nevertheless very clear. So after having discussed and approved the Furundzija trial judgement it explains that: "Subsequently, in the Tadic judgement, the Appeals Chamber briefly considered the liability of one person for acts of another person where the first person has been charged with aiding and abetting that other person in the commission of a crime. This was the context -- this was in the context of contrasting that liability with the liability of a person charged with acting pursuant to a common purpose or design with another person to commit a crime, and for that reason that judgement does not purport to be a complete statement of the liability of the person charged with aiding and abetting." And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 600 -- sorry, 164, the Aleksovski appeals judgement went on to clearly state -- set out the actus reus element for aiding and abetting in a way which did not include specific direction. And further, this can -- that it did not consider specific direction to be an element can also see when it applied the aiding and abetting standard to the facts of the Aleksovski case. I refer to paragraphs 168 and 169. So the Appeals Chamber at the time did not see any contradiction between the Furundzija trial judgement and the Tadic appeal judgement elements of aiding and abetting liability. It did not understand the Tadic appeal judgement as a definitive statement on aiding and abetting. It did not understand the Tadic appeal judgement as adding a distinction -- I'm sorry, to adding a distinct requirement of specific direction. The Perisic appeal judgement, however, goes back to Tadic and offers an alternative interpretation of the specific direction language which is the one that the Aleksovski appeal judgement excluded. In the same way, the Perisic appeal judgement goes back to the Blagojevic appeal judgement and offers an interpretation which was explicitly rejected by the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic and Lukic. And then it goes on to incorrectly interpret the Appeals Chamber's judgements in Mrksic and Lukic, despite their explicit rejection of specific direction as an element of aiding and abetting. The Perisic appeal judgement interprets the Blagojevic appeals judgement paragraph 189 as endorsing the existence of a specific direction element in the actus reus of aiding and abetting. That's in paragraphs 31 and 32. The Perisic appeal judgement's interpretation was, however, rejected by the Appeals Chamber in both Mrksic and Lukic, in which the appellants argued that specific direction was required as an element and that it had not been fulfilled in those cases. This was therefore extensively briefed in both cases. In Mrksic the appellant argued that he could not be convicted of aiding and abetting because his omissions were specifically directed to [sic] assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the perpetration of the crimes that he had been convicted of -- that he were not specifically convicted of. The Perisic appeal judgement misapprehends the Mrksic appeal judgement when at paragraph 33 it states that the Mrksic Appeals Chamber never [sic] discussed specific direction in the context of mens rea. This is incorrect. I'm sorry, that it only discussed -- only discussed it in the context of mens rea. This is incorrect. While Sljivancanin had raised the issue as a mens rea issue, the Appeals Chamber emphasised that "Sljivancanin misapprehends the mens rea standard applicable to aiding and abetting" and clarified that it should have been raised as an actus reus issue. The Appeals Chamber then explicitly rejected his argument, finding that specific direction was "not an essential ingredient of the actus reus of aiding and abetting," Mrksic appeal judgement paragraph 159. There is nothing ambiguous about this express rejection. Furthermore, the question of whether specific direction was an element of aiding and abetting was directly in issue and had to be decided by the Appeals Chamber. Its rejection of specific direction was an essential part of its reasoning and was not a mere passing reference, as it was put in the appeals judgement in Perisic, because the point had to be decided to affirm the conviction. And the point was again affirmed -- confirmed in the Lukic appeal judgement paragraph 424, where the Appeals Chamber said: "In Mrksic and Sljivancanin the Appeals Chamber has clarified that specific direction is not an essential ingredient of the actus reus of aiding and abetting" and then it finds that there are -- there is no cogent reason to depart from this jurisprudence. The Perisic Appeals Chamber's attempt to distinguish or reconcile these judgements with its own preferred interpretation of the law at paragraphs 32 to 36 is untenable given the Mrksic and Lukic Appeals Chamber's plain language rejecting specific direction. Further, like in Blagojevic, the Appeals Chambers in Mrksic and Lukic did not conduct any assessment as to whether a specific direction finding was in fact implicit in the substantial effect and knowledge findings by the Trial Chamber. Moreover, both the dissenting opinions of Judge Guney at paragraphs 10 and 11 and of Judge Agius in Lukic confirmed that the Appeals Chamber's judgements in these two cases were plainly rejecting specific direction as an element of aiding and abetting. In sum, Your Honours, the Perisic appeal judgement's finding that specific direction is an element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting ignores the specific findings in the Aleksovski appeal judgement about the meaning of Tadic; it misinterprets Blagojevic in a manner which has been explicitly denied by the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic and Lukic. The Appeals Chamber's flawed analysis in Perisic should be departed from. And, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber should find that the serious misinterpretation of the Tribunal's long-standing jurisprudence rejecting specific direction is a cogent reason to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement. The third cogent reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- I wonder whether it's the right time for us to stop here since you are going to the third element of your submission --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, we can do that and then continue after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marcussen, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So, Your Honours, I'm turning to the third cogent reason. As the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber pointed out: "The fundamental mandate of the Tribunal to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law cannot be achieved if the accused and the Prosecution do not have the assurance of certainty and predictability in the application of the applicable law." Paragraph 113(ii). A third cogent reason to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement is that it introduces vague concepts which lead to considerable uncertainties and practices as illustrated by my learned friend's arguments this morning. The Perisic appeal judgement introduces new elements into the law of aiding and abetting specific direction and the proximity/remoteness of an accused which has not been applied before. Parties, the Prosecution, Chambers, in this Tribunal and others will now have to grapple with their application. These new concepts are unclear and problematic. The Perisic appeal judgement does not explain what specific direction as an objective element actually is, but simply states that it is a culpable link, paragraphs 37, 38, and 44. Further, there appear to be considerable disagreement between the Judges in their separate and dissenting opinions. Four out of five Judges in the Perisic Appeals Chamber suggest that specific direction is more akin to a mens rea element, Judges Meron and Agius in their separate opinion at paragraph 4; Judge Liu dissenting at paragraph 2 and footnote 7; Judge Ramaroson, separate opinion paragraphs 7 and 9. And in the application of specific direction to the facts of the Perisic case, the Appeals Chamber appears to consider it a cognitive element going beyond knowledge of assistance seeking purpose, at paragraph 69. The implication of the Perisic appeal judgement is that the culpable link will require evidence that the aider and abettor's mens rea exceeded the knowledge standard to something akin to purpose. Yet, the Perisic appeal judgement reasserts that the mens rea for aiding and abetting is knowledge, not purpose, at paragraph 48, as established by the long standing jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The apparent contradiction is difficult to understand or to reconcile in practice. The Perisic appeal judgement also blurs the lines between aiding and abetting and JCE, thus undermining the purpose of aiding and abetting liability. If an aider and abettor now has to specifically direct his assistance to a crime, then there is no difference in the mental state of an aider and abettor and the JCE members who share the common purpose. The Perisic appeal judgement also creates considerable uncertainty because it introduces a new notion of remoteness without any basis in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. In order to distinguish the prior judgements which did not explicitly apply a specific direction requirement, the Perisic Appeals Chamber states that the accused in those previous judgements were proximate aider and abettors such that a specific direction finding could have been implicit in the findings regarding other aiding and abetting elements, at paragraph 38 and in footnote 100. In doing so, it sets two evidentiary standards for aiding and abetting, one for a proximate aider and abettor which do not require explicit consideration and reasoning for one of the elements; and a different one for a remote aider and abettor, where explicit considerations and reasons must be given. And, Your Honours, the confusion was illustrated this morning. My learned friends understand the specific direction element to require that the accused was present when the crimes were being committed. We submit that that's not the case. Somebody like Krstic who was convicted as an aider and abettor, for example, was not present when the crimes were committed, but that this issue come up certainly shows how confusing the situation has now become. It is also confusing because proximity is not defined -- is not determinative of the nature or impact of assistance nor of a contributor's knowledge or frame of mind. For example, a remote perpetrator may be able to recognise a wider pattern of crimes or the systematic nature of crimes which he is assisting and may be able to make much more substantial contributions or assistance in crimes. Furthermore, the Appeals Chamber did not indicate where the boundaries between remoteness and proximity might lie. It only indicated that it is a fact-based analysis which "will depend on the individual circumstances of the case," and that relevant factors include significant temporal distance and geographical distance. However, it also stated that this list is not exhaustive, paragraph 40. These uncertainties may lead to serious problems in practice as individuals will not be able to understand when their acts may lead to liability. Trial Chambers may also have difficulties applying the test imposed by the Perisic appeal judgement. The Appeals Chamber should find the problems and uncertainties created by the Perisic appeal judgement provide a cogent reason to depart from it. And if Your Honours will excuse me just for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now turn to the fourth cogent reason and I will be returning to Judge Liu's question as well -- sorry, maybe there's a question beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, before that could I put a question to you. I think this morning the appellant submits that it was necessary to establish the accused was present at each specific places where a crime is committed so that to establish the aiding and abetting responsibility of the accused. And I understand that your position is the remoteness or proximity is not an essential element in the actus reus of the aiding and abetting. Maybe just because of this question of remoteness the Appeals Chamber of Perisic case introduced the "specific direction" elements in this aspect. Do you have anything to say in this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly agree that the Perisic judgement could be read in that way, and I would submit that raises an additional serious issue with that judgement. We submit that it cannot be the case that different legal standards apply to accused at different levels or different distances, whatever that remoteness means, from a crime. There must be one legal standard that applies to all, that must be a fundamental principle that also this Tribunal applies. But I agree with that it -- the Perisic judgement could be seen as introducing this element for specific type of cases. As I said, we submit that that would be highly problematic if that's actually what it is. That cannot be the law if there are different standards for different accused. As I will get back to in a little bit in answering -- when we get to cogent reason number four, we also submit that there is no reason to introduce such new standards to deal with a specific problem because the existing elements of aiding and abetting safe-guard against any unreasonable convictions. The sufficient -- the existing elements provide -- set such a high threshold that there's not a risk that just anybody who contributes -- who assists, say, a foreign government or insurgency forces will be unreasonably convicted. And we understand, of course, the context is that it's unfortunately known that in many armed conflicts there are elements who might commit crimes. And I think we all understand that it's -- it may be a concern if just the fact that it is known that somebody may commit a crime, somebody who provide assistance to the army can now suddenly be held responsible as an aider and abettor in that crime. But really the high standard we have for aiding and abetting in the jurisprudence safe-guard against those kind of situations, just as somebody who legitimately sold handguns isn't found to be an aider and abettor in every single robbery that may be committed with that weapon that was sold. I hope that was of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Your Honours, the fourth cogent reason is that the Perisic appeal judgement undermines the respect for international humanitarian law. Allowing persons to engage in conduct they know will substantially contribute to a crime because it is not their specific aim to do so risks undermining international humanitarian law. The Perisic appeal judgement, as I mentioned, give rise to what appears to be two fundamental implications. First, the judgement expressly states that the aider and abettor must specifically direct his acts towards a crime or crimes; and second, from the actual findings of that case when the Appeals Chamber applied specific direction to the Perisic case, it appears that a remote aider and abettor who both knows of the substantial likelihood that his acts will assist crimes and whose conduct does, in fact, substantially assist in those crimes will not be considered to have met the elements of aiding and abetting -- the element of specific direction. What is the outcome of this? It means that a remote aider and abettor who both knowingly and substantially contributes to widespread and systematic crimes will escape liability for aiding and abetting. Your Honours, this impunity gap cannot be accepted. And worse, the Perisic appeals judgement appears to require assistance to a purely criminal organisation in order for a remote aider and abettor to attract criminal responsibility. Both governments -- but governments, armies, security forces, insurgency and rebel movements will hardly ever be purely criminal. By introducing a requirement that contributions must be to purely criminal organisations, the impunity gap becomes so huge that little is actually left of aiding and abetting responsibility for remote perpetrators in practice. The customary international law standard of aiding and abetting promotes the respect for international humanitarian law. The Perisic appeal judgement undermines it. The two elements of the customary international law standard of aiding and abetting ensures that there is no risk that anyone will be unreasonably convicted. Only when it's proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused know of the substantial likelihood that his conduct would assist in the commission of serious international crimes and when it's proven beyond a reasonable doubt that his assistance actually had a substantial effect on the commission of those crimes can he be held responsible as an aider and abettor. This was the question, I believe, that Your Honour, Judge Liu, put. The fact that there is a risk that sending troops or providing equipment will lead to crime does not mean that a person is prohibited from assisting a war effort or otherwise legitimate operations and will not be held liable as an aider and abettor if he does so. There are no safe-guards in customary international law of -- in the customary international law standard of substantial effect and knowledge of assistance to crimes to avoid this. First, the standard of knowledge is quite high. It is not sufficient to know of a risk of crimes. The accused but know about -- must know that crimes are probably going to be committed. In particular, if a person takes reasonable measures to ensure that his assistance will not be used to commit crimes, he will not know that crimes will probably be committed nor that his assistance will probably assist in any such crimes. And such measures may vary from case to case, but could, for example, include obtaining guarantees that the help will not be used to commit crimes, obtaining guarantees that the receiving forces will take all necessary measures to prevent and punish crimes before help is provided, could also be providing training on international humanitarian law before or as a condition for providing assistance, it could be stopping or temporarily ceasing the provision of assistance if crimes are permitted but not punished, it could amount to asking for the return of material or manpower provided if it is used to commit crimes, and the persons who received the assistance failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent and punish crimes. There are many steps that a provider of assistance can take: To, first of all, ensure that crimes are not being committed, and taking those steps will make it very reasonable for that person to believe that crimes are not being committed and certainly not being committed with -- somehow with the assistance of the -- through the means that are being provided by the assistance. And therefore, there are sufficient safe-guards to avoid unreasonable results. But moreover, and very importantly, such steps would reduce the prevalence of crimes and encourage adherence to international humanitarian law. If such steps do not work and those receiving the aid still use it to commit crimes, then the persons who knowingly continued to provide assistance in these circumstances may be liable for aiding and abetting those crimes. Equally, if a person knows that no means would ever be sufficient to prevent the commission of large-scale massive systematic crimes, they should refrain from providing the assistance or run the risk of being held criminally liable as aiders and abettors. The customary international law standard on aiding and abetting promotes the respect for international humanitarian law; the Perisic appeal judgement undermines it. All of the above shows that there are cogent reasons to depart from the Perisic appeals judgement. It is wrong in customary international law, it wrongly interprets the Appeals Chamber case law, and very seriously it creates uncertainty and problems, and, maybe worse of all, it undermines the adherence to international humanitarian law contrary to the interests of international justice. The Appeals Chamber should reiterate that specific direction is not a distinct aiding and abetting requirement or that if it is involved in the actus reus it is necessarily included within the element of substantial effect. Now, should the Appeals Chamber require further assistance on cogent reasons, the Prosecution can prepare a supplemental written brief on this issue. If there are no questions on this, I shall move on to the final part of my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if the Appeals Chamber decides that there are no cogent reasons to depart from the Perisic appeal judgement, then the Appeals Chamber may have to consider: One, whether the Trial Chamber should have entered explicit findings regarding the specific direction element of the actus reus for aiding and abetting; and two, if it did not have to make such findings, whether the Trial Chamber's findings implicitly included this element. And actually, I think Your Honours would have to make those determinations because it was specifically raised by my learned colleagues this morning. Contrary to what my learned friends submitted this morning, the Trial Chamber did not have to make explicit findings regarding specific direction as an element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting in this case. This is because General Lazarevic is a proximate aider and abettor rather than a remote one, under Perisic paragraph 39. First, whereas General Perisic was remote in that he was an officer in a foreign army outside the chain of command of those who committed the crimes in Srebrenica and Sarajevo, General Lazarevic was the corps commander of the VJ soldiers perpetrating the forcible displacements in Kosovo. He had the authority over all Pristina Corps members and the power to plan VJ activities and operations in Kosovo, Volume III, paragraph 905 [sic]. He is akin to Krstic, a commander who permitted troops and resources under his command to assist in crimes, who was recognised by the Perisic appeal judgement as a proximity aider and abettor, in footnote 100. Indeed, the Perisic Appeals Chamber placed great importance on the fact that Perisic had no de jure and de facto command over the VRS in Bosnia to establish Perisic's remoteness, paragraphs 42 and -- paragraphs 42 and 46. Second, the Perisic appeal judgement, paragraph 38, held that proximity is established when the accused is physically present during the planning or commission of a crime. Lazarevic was physically present and significantly contributed to the planning and execution of the joint operations which cleared whole villages of Albanian civilians. The period from January to March 1999 was devoted to planning of joint VJ-MUP operations, Volume I, paragraph 1017. Lazarevic worked closely with Pavkovic on these plans and the resultant Joint Command Orders, Volume I, paragraphs 1034 -- sorry, 1037 to 1038. The campaign to forcibly expel the Kosovo Albanian population was carried out through these joint operations. General Lazarevic also issued at least 16 Joint Command orders between March and April 1999. I will provide examples which show how these orders, joint orders, were implemented -- and implemented the common criminal plan to forcibly expel Kosovo Albanians. As the Trial Chamber found, several of those orders correspond to crime sites in the indictment, Volume I, paragraphs 1122 and paragraph 1123. Moreover, General Lazarevic was present on the ground "on the front line of the action" as he put it and quoted in Volume III, paragraph 924. He regularly visited and encouraged troops before and after joint operations that he planned and commanded and which were implemented with excessive force, targeting whole villages of civilians and driving out the Kosovo Albanian residents. He was with Pavkovic "most of the time," Volume III, paragraph 838. He is akin to Brdjanin and Simic about -- be it civilian leaders in their region and their municipality respectively, whom the Perisic Appeals Chamber also recognised as proximity aiders and abettors in footnote 100. The Trial Chamber, therefore, did not have to make specific findings regarding the specific direction element of the actus reus of aiding and abetting under the Perisic appeal judgement paragraph 37 [sic]. And in fact, given Lazarevic's proximity and intimate involvement in the planning and execution of these joint operations, you can see that the Trial Chamber's findings regarding General Lazarevic's contributions implicitly included specific direction. The Trial Chamber noted "the political and military leadership of the FRY and Serbia ... treated the Kosovo Albanian population in its entirety as enemies of the state, despite the fact that the KLA formed only a very small part of that population," Volume III, paragraph 91. The joint VJ-MUP operations made no distinction between the KLA and the Kosovo Albanian population. Two examples, the joint VJ-MUP operations in Orahovac and Reka valley illustrate that Lazarevic's contributions were directed to operations which were planned and executed to clear whole villages and areas of Kosovo Albanians. Orahovac is in the south-west of Kosovo. One of the villages targeted in the Orahovac operation was Celine village. In March 1999, Celine village consisted of around 250 homes. It was situated not far from the Djakovica forward command post, Volume II, paragraphs 303, 333 to 335. It was explicitly mentioned and targeted by Lazarevic's Joint Command order dated the 23rd of March, 1999, Volume II, paragraph 296. General Lazarevic ordered the 549th Motorised Brigade to deploy at a line, and together with the MUP attack, break up, and destroy the KLA in Celine and other villages. General Lazarevic's order went down the chain of command. The 549th motorised Brigade the same day ordered its units to cut off and destroy the KLA in the village of Celine, paragraph 297 of Volume II. There was, however, little or no KLA presence or threat in this village, Volume II, paragraph 304. And in reality these orders were orders for the attack on the Kosovo Albanian population in Celine, as the findings regarding the attack clearly shows. From the early morning of the 25th of March, Celine village was surrounded by VJ tanks, armoured vehicles, and armoured personnel carriers. Between 5.00 and 5.30 a.m., the VJ began shelling the village and continued to do so on and off until about 9.00 p.m. at night. A day of shelling of 200 homes. VJ soldiers and MUP forces entered the village. Their operations were co-ordinated. The soldiers had hand-held radios and they were given orders through these radios, Volume II, paragraphs 310 to 314. The VJ forces and MUP forces looted and torched the village, also setting fire to the mosque. They set up manned points around the village and shots were fired during the night to scare the villagers, Volume II, paragraph 311. The forces went house to house conducting searches and pulling out everyone they found. Some of those found were murdered, including women and children, Volume II, paragraphs 315, 321, 329 to 335. A large group of civilians were found hiding in the woods by policemen. The men were separated from the women and children. Policemen took their possessions and identification guards. Their identification cards were thrown into a pile and burned. The groups were made to walk through the village towards Prizren at gunpoint. Later these civilians were put on trucks, driven to the border, where they were forced to walk to Albania, Volume II, paragraphs 323 to 325 and 334. Following the operations, reports were sent up the chain of command. For example, Prosecution Exhibit P2019 which confirms that VJ forces "blocked and cleansed" Celine, Volume II, paragraph 364 and also paragraphs 301 and Volume III, paragraph 857. The operation was planned, ordered, and was reported back as implemented in accordance with those plans and orders. Despite the large number of civilians killed in this joint operation as set out in Volume II, paragraph 335, 381 and 382 and 433, and the massive number of Albanians who fled in fear or were ordered across the border which General Lazarevic knew, Volume III, paragraph 849, no one was prosecuted as a result, Volume III, paragraph 864 to 869. And the same soldiers were used again in future operations. Inevitably the same pattern repeated over and over and over again. For example, units of the 349th [sic] Motorised Brigade one month later participated in the Reka Valley Operation during which the VJ and the MUP swept through the valley expelling all Albanians. This is my second example. Sorry, and I seem to have misspoken, it was units of the 549th Motorised Brigade who participated in the operation again. Both Witnesses Peraj and Kotur were VJ soldiers provided evidence of meetings to organise and co-ordinate the operation to cleanse Reka Valley. Both spoke of receiving oral orders for the operation, Volume II, paragraph 600 -- no, sorry, paragraph 169 and 173. In addition, Witnesses K90 and K73, both again VJ soldiers, also described receiving oral orders to cleanse the Reka Valley by expelling Kosovo Albanians, Volume II, paragraph 176 and 230. And, Your Honours, this morning my learned friends addressed the evidence of witness -- of both these witnesses, K90 and K73. Contrary to my learned friends' submissions, the issues that were raised in relation to K90, namely, the allegation that he changed his testimony, was specifically dealt with by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber found that he tried to minimise his evidence and explain -- gave reasons why it came to the conclusions that it did too -- that it did. My learned colleagues have not shown that those findings were unreasonable; it has just invited Your Honours to accept its interpretation of the evidence. And I will refer Your Honours to Volume II, paragraph 34 [sic] and paragraph 133 -- sorry, 53, where these issues -- where the issues relating to K90 are discussed. And contrary to the submissions made this morning, K73 did speak of orders to cleanse the -- cleanse areas of Kosovo Albanians, and the reasons for those findings are clearly set out in the judgement at Volume II, paragraph 176. Your Honours, during this operation, VJ and the MUP swept down the Reka Valley from north to south in two days, terrorising and driving out all of the civilian population as they went. And, Your Honours -- Your Honours, on your screen is now Prosecution Exhibit P326. It was used with several witnesses. This is a one that was tendered through Witness Nike Peraj. As Your Honours can see, this was a joint operation. It had the flanks -- on the flanks of the valley were VJ positions and MUP positions. The operation took place right in front of the VJ Joint Command position -- joint -- sorry, forward command post. There was a MUP command post. And groups, units, of VJ soldiers and MUP went down through the valley in the course of two days. And on the map you can see the approximate line where the operation stopped on the 27th of April, 1999, and then continued on the 28th, forcing civilians in front of it down through the valley. On the first day, K73's unit "expelled hundreds of Kosovo Albanians and set their homes on fire," Volume II, paragraph 229. VJ and the MUP -- VJ and MUP forces surrounded villages, ordering women to leave and go to Albania, and then shot the men and boys. Their homes were burnt down. And at VJ and MUP check-points set up at the southern end of the valley, any remaining men were separated out and the women and children had their identification cards seized before being seized -- excuse me, before being forced to go to Albania under threat of death, paragraph 230. And Your Honours can see, as I mentioned, the check-points, for example, that I mentioned circled on this map and the red lines as indicated, indicate two columns of refugees that are described in the -- of Kosovo Albanians that are described in the evidence in the [indiscernible]. These all-inclusive clearances took place despite the fact that there was no significant KLA presence there, Volume II, paragraph 230. Four VJ soldiers involved gave evidence that they were under orders to expel the Kosovo Albanian civilian population from the valley, discussed in Volume II at paragraphs 169, 173, 176, and 230. Witness K33's [sic] testimony quoted at Volume II, paragraph 1172, confirmed that what his order required him to do in this joint operation and what -- and that it was not to target the KLA. And I once again need to correct myself - I apologise, Your Honours - the witness is Witness K73. The instructions that K73 had received he set out as being: "... we expelled them all from the baby in the cradle to the elderly people in wheelchairs." General Lazarevic visited the 125th Motorised Brigade on the 29th of April, 1999, immediately after their involvement with the Reka Valley operation. Zivanovic reported to Lazarevic on the operation, Volume III, paragraph 842 and 856. Lazarevic took no measures against the VJ forces involved in the comprehensive forcible expulsions in Reka Valley. No one was prosecuted for these events, Volume III, paragraph 870. And again, after the Reka Valley operation, joint operations continued unchanged and unhindered. For example, the VJ-MUP joint action attack on the village of Dubrava in May 1999 that followed the same pattern. The villagers fled in fear or were killed, including a female and a child, Volume II, paragraph 1141 and 1149. The operations in Orahovac and Reka Valley are but two examples which illustrate how, in fact, joint operations by the VJ and MUP were designed to attack the Kosovo Albanian population. Volume II is replete with other examples covering 13 municipalities all over Kosovo. General Lazarevic's substantial assistance, encouragement, and moral support was directed at and related specifically to these joint operations, which treated the whole Kosovo Albanian population as the enemy. When Lazarevic planned and executed these operations, when he sent his troops and weapons to areas where there was little or no KLA presence, when he inspected the troops in the field who had just carried out forcible expulsions, when he failed to take measures specifically against forcible displacements, paragraph 925 of Volume III, there was no way he could have thought that he was assisting legitimate warfare. He knew his assistance was directed and substantially facilitated the campaign of forcible expulsions. For these reasons the Appeals Chamber should not accept General Lazarevic's argument that he only contributed to the war efforts of his country. Clearly, as the VJ commander in the field his contributions were significantly directed to assist in the commission of crimes that he was convicted of. Such was Lazarevic's intimate and protracted involvement and proximity that there was a direct, close, and culpable link between his contributions and the crimes. Your Honours, the -- my learned colleagues this morning suggested that General Lazarevic was merely carrying out his duties. I would note that in the Blagojevic appeal judgement at paragraph 800 -- 189, the Appeals Chamber specifically held that when somebody knowingly contributes to the commission of a crime, the fact that this is done in -- pursuant to a duty does not alleviate that person of responsibility. I need, maybe, to correct one thing that I said this morning about paragraph -- the submission by my learned colleague regarding paragraph 906 in the judgement. I may have said -- in Volume III. I may have said that there was a finding of intent in that paragraph. That is incorrect. What it was is it said that General Lazarevic was aware of acts of violence and expulsions. And also, the assessment of K90's evidence is found in Volume II at paragraph 74 and not 34 as I said. With those clarifications and unless I may assist Your Honours any further, this would conclude the Prosecution's response to General Lazarevic's appeal and the questions put by Your Honours before the hearing. For further issues that I have not addressed today, I refer Your Honours to the detailed responses in the Prosecution's response brief to General Lazarevic's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, with your leave. My learned friend Mr. Marcussen was dealing with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal for a good part of his address and also the legal practice relating to a specific issue, the issue of specific direction and the requirement that it be part of the actus reus of the accused for aiding and abetting or for -- or part of the mens rea of the accused. Of course it is very difficult immediately after the address when my learned friend Mr. Marcussen quoted and cited precedents, it's difficult to reply on one's feet after hearing such arguments. But even -- despite that I'm still going to state my position on all of these issues to a limited extent because of the requirement for me to provide my reply immediately after the address by Mr. Marcussen. It seems to me and perhaps I'm wrong, I apologise, or perhaps it just sounds like that, that the practice of the International Criminal Tribunal and customary law on the matter of specific direction simply is a singular thing and the appeals judgement in the Perisic case deviates from that. If this is the position, I think that this is what can be concluded from the address by Mr. Marcussen and I cannot agree with that. The judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Perisic case is not the only such judgement which treats this matter in the way it does. If you permit me just briefly, I am going to deal with examples that my learned friend Mr. Marcussen did not mention. On several occasions the Appeals Chamber defined the actus reus for aiding and abetting as acts specifically directed towards the aiding, encouragement, or providing moral support to the principal perpetrators of a crime which have a significant effect on the execution of the crime. When I say this, I refer to the to the Tadic appeals judgement, paragraph 229; the Vasiljevic appeals judgement, paragraph 102; the Blagojevic appeals judgement, paragraph 127; the Kvocka appeals judgement, paragraph 89; the Blaskic appeals judgement, paragraph 45; the Rukundo appeals judgement paragraph 52 -- I apologise. I'm now moving to an overview of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal where there is a consistent approach by the Appeals Chambers on this particular standard. First of all, this standard for specific direction was articulated for the first time in the Tadic appeals judgement, but that concept, the concept of specific direction, continues to be a part of the actus reus arguments for aiding and abetting, and it can be found in other judgements as well. Other than that, the International Criminal Court -- I would also like to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber to the Rukundo judgement -- appeals judgement, paragraph 52, which also deals with specific direction; then Kalimanzira appeals judgement, paragraphs 74 and 76 and 86 -- 74 and 86; Muguniya [phoen] - I apologise if I'm mispronouncing the names - this is the appeals judgement, paragraph 79; Seromba, appeals judgement, paragraph 47; Nahimana appeals judgement, paragraph 482; and the Ntakirutimana appeals judgement, paragraph 530. Again, I apologise if I mispronounce the names. So there are numerous judgements by Appeals Chambers which deal with the issue of specific direction and which treat this particular area. My learned friend, Mr. Marcussen, tried to simplify one of the requisite conditions with regard to the remoteness of the perpetrator, suggesting that any perpetrator who is remote from the site of the commission of a crime would be exculpated from responsibility. I believe that this is quite a simplification of that position. With all due respect to Mr. Marcussen, remoteness is one of the elements that has to be established. It's quite clear that somebody who is remote from the place of commission of a crime can fulfil the requisite criteria for actus reus and for mens rea for the crime of aiding and abetting. However, it is necessary to establish all the other elements of actus reus and mens rea. Simply, the application of this principle would not have any consequences in terms of the perpetrators who just by the nature of the fact that they are remote from the scene of the crime would be exculpated on the basis of that. My learned friend Mr. Marcussen even said that -- I apologise, Your Honours. As for the jurisprudence regarding the principle of specific direction, with all due respect, I believe that my learned friend Mr. Marcussen did not articulate adequate arguments in view of the fact that this problem has been considered to a large extent by international tribunals and that the concept is known in international customary and humanitarian law and it would need to be applied in situations of crimes which are specifically the subject of review by this Appeals Chamber. Furthermore, my colleague Mr. Marcussen also referred to the fact that in our oral submissions we referred to the question of the standard of the objective or goal of mens rea and referring to the Rome Statute Article 25(3)(c). The Defence believes that it did not overstep the grounds of appeal because one of the grounds of appeal is the erroneous finding by the Trial Chamber of the mens rea of the accused Lazarevic in relation to aiding and abetting of the crime of deportation and forcible displacement. The standard of the goal or purpose was applied also in some other judgements, for example, of the transitional administration of the United Nations in the year 2000 which constitutes a new practice and I think that it was completely justified as well, also with respect to the Defence referring to this element of the mens rea and that this is also in the interest of justice and does not exceed the bounds of what we refer to as the ground of appeal of the erroneous findings of the Trial Chamber in relation to the mens rea for this type of criminal act which we refer to in our appeal brief. Today at the very beginning of his address, my learned friend Mr. Marcussen said that my colleague Mr. Cepic when -- actually, he responded to our grounds of appeal. He said that we cited evidence which is not linked to the relevant parts and he cited the example of Srbica, giving dates from April and March 1999. And that for that reason we made a mistake as to the relevant time-period of these events. My colleague Mr. Cepic presented a clear contradiction precisely for the relevant period of the indictment when we're talking about Volume III, paragraph 905 of the judgement, citing an example for the 28th of March, 1999, and the area of Srbica. So we hold that this argument by the Prosecutor does not stand. All the other presented evidence refer to the relevant period. Other than that, the Prosecution did not provide any other evidence to substantiate his allegations regarding the disciplinary measures and acts taken to shed light on the crimes. Here we presented numerous direct evidence before you which would be difficult to find in any other case before this Tribunal, indicating that General Lazarevic did everything in his power so that all alleged perpetrated crimes by members of the VJ would be thoroughly investigated and processed. The responsibility, as we mentioned, for further processing lay in the hands of the judicial organs so that all of this would lead to the reasonable conclusion that General Lazarevic in everything acted in accordance with the law and the constitution. When one takes measures to process the perpetrators of a criminal act and when this processing is supposed to be undertaken by the judicial organs, then the assertion by my friend Mr. Marcussen is superfluous that the measures provided for under customary law were not applied by General Lazarevic. Your Honours, my colleague Mr. Marcussen stated also that General Lazarevic was responsible also because he knew about the crimes which were committed in 1998. He knew about the mass displacements and forcible displacements in 1998, knew that members of the Army of Yugoslavia which he allegedly used later in 1999 frequently committed crimes which had, as a consequence, a significant or substantial displacement of the population. These assertions absolutely do not stand. I am just going to draw your attention to a number of Prosecution witnesses, foreign observers, whose mission it was in 1998 specifically to observe and monitor the situation in the field. So Prosecution witness Mr. Ciaglinski on page 6910 of the transcript said that the actions of the VJ in the border belt area were carried out correctly. I remind that the border belt area is the area where General Lazarevic was in 1998 as the Chief of Staff at the time of the Pristina Corps. Witness Ciaglinski said that he had the opportunity to read numerous reports drafted by members of his mission, and these reports did not contain any remarks regarding the conduct of the army. And you can find this on transcript page 6894 to 6895. In January 1999 Witness Ciaglinski testified that he had the opportunity to speak with local Albanians in the Junik border belt village, who personally told him that they did not have any problems with members of the army. And you can find this on transcript page 6896. Witness Ciaglinski concludes at the end that -- going back a little bit: "When I talk about the VJ certainly during most of my time in Kosovo the VJ behaved correctly. It was not using excessive force until the last few weeks of March 1999." This is on transcript page 6929. Prosecution Witness Maisonneuve said that his experience was that the Army of Yugoslavia acted very professionally. Witness Shaun Byrnes, a member of the American mission, when asked about excessive use of force, bombing, and the torching of houses, some cases in 1998, said that his clear impression was and that he could state that quite clearly was that the Army of Yugoslavia was not involved in such activity. He also says concerning the time I spent in Kosovo and as far as 1998 is concerned, that is August and all of September, he personally never saw the Army of Yugoslavia being involved in that kind of activity, nor did he receive any such information from his subordinates; 12150 is the transcript page reference. There is also numerous evidence that indicates that there is no reliable evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that General Lazarevic in 1998 as Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps who was at the forward command post near the border with Albania had any knowledge about possible individual cases of excessive use of force in 1998. There is no evidence that General Lazarevic knew or had to know about Resolution 1299, that in October 1998 cautioned that FRY forces were using force. What may have been relevant for General Lazarevic was, first of all, the assessment of General Perisic. And the Prosecution says that this is a renegade general who opposed Milosevic. 3D757 is the document where he pointed out on the 29th of September, 1998, that in actions in Kosovo the Army of Yugoslavia was carrying out its obligations in fighting against terrorism in a professional manner. He added that the Army of Yugoslavia, the Army of Yugoslavia through the Pristina Corps, took all necessary measures, all necessary measures, to protect the country. Your Honours, when my learned friend Mr. Marcussen said that General Lazarevic in 1999 used the army, or rather, the troops that did what I read out to you in 1998 and what the foreign observers assessed as well, he made a major mistake. In our brief we proffered to the Chamber ample evidence showing that in 1999 when the aggression was supposed to start, the aggression by NATO forces against the FRY, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia reached a decision on manning the units of the Pristina Corps. I wish to note that a Prosecution witness, Colonel Zyrapi, who was the Chief of Staff of the KLA, said himself that in the beginning of the NATO bombing the KLA had a personnel level that was twice as high as the Pristina Corps. The Pristina Corps had 10.000 members at the time. As their personnel levels were raised by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, it became 50.000. So this fact alone cannot support the position of the Prosecution that General Lazarevic used the forces that he knew committed crimes in 1998 in 1999. First of all, he could not have done such a thing in terms of the position he held; and secondly, in 1999 when the NATO campaign started the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia - and we indicated that in detail in our appeal - increased personnel levels in the Pristina Corps many-fold at that. My learned friend Mr. Marcussen, my learned friend Mr. Marcussen, also at the end of his remarks mentioned an incident in the village of Celine, and he referred to the alleged participation of the Army of Yugoslavia in the commission of crimes. In our appeal, paragraph 252, we analyse in detail the evidence related to this incident. I would briefly like to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber that Witness Bislim Zyrapi, Chief of Staff of the KLA, confirmed that the thrust of the Serb forces' attack was against the KLA and in the village of Pirane which is the neighbouring village of Celine. I quote: "From Pirane to the Djakovica, the Djakovica cross-roads and Bela Crkva, the attack started in the early morning hours of the 25th of March, 1999, and there was combat activity. This is what I wish to point out. Before the artillery attack started" -- correction. "After the artillery attack started, we wanted to move the population from that area for reasons of safety. The forces of the KLA together with the population started withdrawing."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Chief of Staff of the KLA as regards this incident - and my learned friend says that it was aimed only against the civilian population - claims that it was KLA forces that were there and that they were moving along with the civilian population and were mixed among the civilian population. I hope that I have a bit more time, five minutes. The Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have to finish your reply in five minutes. So we adjourn at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I was afraid that I had stolen a minute or two by accident, that is. So the very last argument that was presented by my learned friend Mr. Marcussen was the operation in the river valley and with regard to that the Defence provides a detailed analysis of everything that happened. Within the time that I still have left, I would just like to refer to what my colleague Mr. Marcussen pointed out. He says that after this operation General Lazarevic went to the 125th Motorised Brigade that was partly only under blockade in terms of this operation and he says that Commander Zivanovic reported to him but General Lazarevic did not take any steps to punish perpetrators of crimes. In the case file you will find the report of Commander Zivanovic and you will see that in the report there is no indication whatsoever of the 125th Motorised Brigade participating in the crime or that any crime had happened. So General Lazarevic did not have any information from his superior officer that in the operation of blockade in which the 125th Brigade participated that any crimes had been committed, that is, and therefore he could not have taken any kind of action. Finally, my colleague Mr. Marcussen says that General Lazarevic closely co-operated in elaborating plans with Commander Pavkovic. Can you imagine a single army anywhere in the world where the command of the Pristina Corps -- rather, any corps commander would not have a co-operation with the army commander, where the army commander would not co-operate with the Chief of General Staff. That is quite logical. The question is just which part of that co-operation would be illegal, anti-constitutional, and which part of that co-operation would be aimed against civilian persons? That is an answer that the trial judgement could not respond to. That is something that the Prosecution could not indicate to us in their reply. Is it sufficient to say merely that General Lazarevic closely co-operated with General Pavkovic? Well, of course. General Pavkovic was commander of the 3rd Army and General Lazarevic was his subordinate in the chain of command. He was the corps commander there. Military hierarchy, per se, is it a crime? Is waging war, per se, a crime? I think that the Prosecution in their reply to our appeal did not assist you in finding arguments in the trial judgement that would indicate that the only reasonable conclusion would be, if looking at all the facts together, that General Lazarevic supported and aided and abetted in the crimes of forcible transfer. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Bakrac. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just one correction in transcript. Page 24 [sic], line 15, instead of word "superior" it has to be "subordinated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I think that's all for today, and that concludes today's hearing. We adjourn these proceedings until tomorrow morning at 9.30 a.m.
